note: Parts knowledge base. The AI's search_parts / part_detail tools look things up here; anything not listed gets flagged by the AI as "not in catalog, verify", and you can add it with add_part. Fields: id short English id; name English name (with common model numbers); cat category (Controllers/Tools/Passives/Inputs/Sensors/Displays/Outputs/Actuators/Communication/Storage/Power/Mechanical & consumables); iface interface (GPIO/PWM/ADC/UART/I2C/SPI/1-Wire/analog/—); volt operating voltage (flags 5V-only parts and whether a level shifter is needed); price rough 2026 USD range at US retailers such as Amazon, Adafruit, SparkFun and DigiKey (estimates for budgeting only; AliExpress is usually cheaper); buy an Amazon-style search phrase, plus a vendor hint where a well-known product exists; lib the library name for platformio.ini lib_deps (owner/name) or the core API; pins the labels printed on the module; wiring one line on connecting it to the STM32F103 Blue Pill (I2C1=PB6 SCL/PB7 SDA, SPI1=PA5 SCK/PA6 MISO/PA7 MOSI, UART1=PA9 TX/PA10 RX, UART2=PA2 TX/PA3 RX, ADC=PA0-PA7 PB0 PB1, PWM=PA0-PA3 PA6-PA10 PB0 PB1 PB6-PB9); snippet minimal working Arduino-style code; pitfalls the mistakes beginners make most often; note a one-line summary.

parts.name: STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill (minimal dev board)
parts.volt: 3.3V logic; power from USB 5V or the 3.3V pin. The ADC pins PA0-PA7, PB0, PB1 are NOT 5V-tolerant; PA8-PA15 and PB2-PB15 can take 5V inputs
parts.buy: STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill development board
parts.pins: 3.3 5V GND PA0-PA15 PB0-PB15 PC13-PC15 SWDIO SWCLK NRST BOOT0 BOOT1
parts.wiring: Four wires to the ST-Link: SWDIO→SWDIO, SWCLK→SWCLK, GND→GND, 3.3V→3.3V. Set both BOOT jumpers to the 0 side (toward the USB port)
pitfalls: If flashing fails with something like "unknown chip id", you most likely got a CH32/GD32 clone chip: add -c "set CPUTAPID 0" to upload_flags to work around it
The onboard LED is on PC13 and lights when you write LOW, the opposite of what you'd expect
The USB port has no serial function by default; to see printouts, buy a separate CH340 adapter. To use USB as a serial port, enable USB CDC in build_flags
parts.note: The starter controller. Cheap, tons of resources, plenty of gotchas; once you've been through them, every other STM32 works the same way

parts.name: Nucleo-F103RB (official ST dev board)
parts.buy: NUCLEO-F103RB development board (also at DigiKey/Mouser)
parts.pins: Arduino female headers D0-D15 A0-A5 + dual-row Morpho pins; LD2 onboard LED = PA5, USER button = PC13
parts.wiring: One Mini-USB cable to your computer and you're done; the board has a built-in ST-Link and virtual COM port. Leave both CN2 jumpers in place
pitfalls: Serial goes through the onboard ST-Link's virtual COM port, not the PA9/PA10 header pins, so don't wire up the wrong place and wait for output
Seven or eight times the price of a Blue Pill; what you're paying for is peace of mind: no programmer needed, no clone-chip worries
parts.note: Official board with built-in ST-Link; the easiest way into STM32, just pricier

parts.name: ESP32 DevKitC (WROOM-32)
parts.volt: 3.3V logic, USB 5V powered; GPIOs are not 5V-tolerant
parts.buy: ESP32 DevKitC WROOM-32 development board
parts.pins: 3V3 5V(VIN) GND EN GPIO0-39 (34-39 are input-only)
parts.wiring: USB cable to your computer; default I2C is GPIO21 SDA / GPIO22 SCL, default UART0 is GPIO1 TX / GPIO3 RX (flashing uses it too)
pitfalls: 2.4GHz WiFi only; if it won't connect, first check whether your router is on the 5GHz band
GPIO6-11 are wired to the onboard flash and can't be used; GPIO34-39 have no output capability
If flashing hangs at Connecting..., hold the BOOT button on the board for a few seconds
parts.note: Go straight to this for anything that needs a network or phone control. It's not an STM32, but PlatformIO works the same way

parts.name: Freenove ESP32-WROVER board (with camera)
parts.volt: 3.3V logic, powered over USB-C 5V; GPIOs are NOT 5V-tolerant, so divide down any 5V output
parts.buy: Freenove ESP32 WROVER CAM board development kit
parts.pins: 3V3 5V GND EN GPIO0-39 (34-39 are input-only; 6-11 are wired to the flash and unusable)
parts.wiring: A USB-C data cable straight to your computer is all you need — no programmer. Default I2C is GPIO21 SDA / GPIO22 SCL; serial runs at 115200
pitfalls: The onboard LED is GPIO2 and is active HIGH (the Blue Pill is active LOW — do not copy that habit across)
Do not upload at 921600 baud: the CH340 cannot keep up and you get "Unable to verify flash chip connection". Drop to 115200
On a Mac with no USB-A port the cable in the kit is useless — you need a C-to-C DATA cable (a charge-only cable will not work)
GPIO6-11 are wired to the onboard flash and cannot be used; GPIO34-39 are input-only
parts.note: The main board for this project. WiFi, Bluetooth and a camera built in, flashes straight over USB-C, no ST-Link needed

parts.name: STM32F411CEU6 Black Pill (WeAct)
parts.volt: 3.3V logic, USB-C 5V powered; ADC pins are not 5V-tolerant
parts.buy: WeAct STM32F411CEU6 Black Pill development board
parts.pins: 3V3 5V GND PA0-PA15 PB0-PB15 PC13-PC15 KEY(PA0) BOOT0 NRST
parts.wiring: USB-C straight to your computer. Hold BOOT0, tap NRST, then release BOOT0 to enter DFU mode; you can then flash without an ST-Link
pitfalls: DFU flashing needs you to enter the mode by hand every time; if that gets annoying, just use an ST-Link
The same board shape also comes as an F401CCU6 version with only 256K flash; it's a couple of dollars cheaper, so check the chip marking before you buy
parts.note: The Blue Pill's big brother: 100MHz, an FPU, twice the flash. Displays and audio don't feel cramped

parts.name: Arduino UNO R3 (compatible board)
parts.volt: 5V logic! Be careful when connecting to 3.3V modules or a Blue Pill
parts.buy: Arduino UNO R3 compatible board CH340 (official UNO R3 also at Arduino/Adafruit/SparkFun)
parts.pins: D0-D13 A0-A5 5V 3.3V GND VIN; D13 onboard LED
parts.wiring: The UNO is 5V logic: when wiring UNO TX to Blue Pill RX, put a 1kΩ+2kΩ voltage divider in between to bring it down to 3.3V; the other way around, the UNO reads the Blue Pill's 3.3V output directly
pitfalls: It's a 5V system; hooking up 3.3V-only modules (many sensors, SD cards, nRF24) will fry them
Only 2K of RAM; drawing graphics on an OLED blows through it fast
It has the most tutorials online, but its pin numbering is completely different from STM32, so remap the pins before copying anything
parts.note: The board with the most tutorials; many module guides and datasheets assume it by default

parts.name: Arduino Nano (compatible board, CH340)
parts.buy: Arduino Nano V3 CH340 with soldered headers
parts.pins: D0-D13 A0-A7 5V 3V3 GND VIN; D13 onboard LED
parts.wiring: Plugs straight into a breadboard; Mini-USB power; like the UNO, use a voltage divider when connecting to 3.3V modules
pitfalls: If upload fails, try board=nanoatmega328 (old bootloader); the old and new bootloaders use different baud rates
The 3V3 pin can only supply 50mA, not enough for a WiFi module
parts.note: The UNO's breadboard-friendly version, still 5V logic

parts.name: ESP8266 NodeMCU (CP2102/CH340)
parts.volt: 3.3V logic, USB 5V powered; A0 max 1V (up to 3.3V through the board's divider)
parts.buy: NodeMCU ESP8266 CH340 development board
parts.pins: 3V3 GND VIN D0-D8 A0 RX TX
parts.wiring: USB cable to your computer; default I2C is D2(GPIO4) SDA / D1(GPIO5) SCL
pitfalls: The D1, D2 labels printed on the board are not the GPIO numbers used in code: D1=GPIO5, D2=GPIO4
Only one ADC and few usable GPIOs; with several sensors you run out of pins
The levels on D3, D4, D8 at power-up affect booting; don't hang anything on those pins that pulls them low
parts.note: The cheapest way to get online; plenty for a project that reports temperature and humidity to your phone

parts.name: ESP32-C3 SuperMini
parts.buy: ESP32-C3 SuperMini development board
parts.pins: 3V3 5V GND GPIO0-10 GPIO20 GPIO21
parts.wiring: USB-C straight in; for serial output over USB add -DARDUINO_USB_CDC_ON_BOOT=1 to build_flags; I2C can use any two pins with Wire.begin(sda, scl)
pitfalls: The onboard ceramic antenna is weak; move a bit away from the router and it drops out, and some batches have an antenna design flaw
Few pins (about a dozen); complex projects will feel the squeeze
parts.note: A fingernail-sized WiFi controller, great for wearables and night-light style projects

parts.name: Raspberry Pi Pico / Pico W (RP2040)
parts.volt: 3.3V logic, USB 5V powered; GPIOs are not 5V-tolerant
parts.buy: Raspberry Pi Pico RP2040 (Adafruit, SparkFun, Micro Center, Amazon)
parts.pins: GP0-GP28 VBUS VSYS 3V3 GND; GP25 onboard LED
parts.wiring: Hold BOOTSEL while plugging in USB; a USB drive appears on your computer. Drag the compiled .uf2 onto it and it's flashed
pitfalls: Only three ADC pins: GP26 GP27 GP28
Also not 5V-tolerant; don't wire it the way you would an UNO
parts.note: Excellent official docs, and it runs MicroPython too; PlatformIO supports it as well

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer (USB-stick style)
parts.volt: Outputs 3.3V (there's also a 5V pin; don't connect it to the Blue Pill's 3.3V)
parts.buy: ST-LINK V2 programmer debugger STM32
parts.pins: 3.3V 5V SWDIO SWCLK GND RST SWIM
parts.wiring: Four female-to-female jumper wires: ST-Link SWDIO→Blue Pill SWDIO(PA13), SWCLK→SWCLK(PA14), GND→GND, 3.3V→3.3V. The pinout is printed on the aluminum shell; go by that
parts.snippet:
; platformio.ini
[env:bluepill]
platform = ststm32
board = bluepill_f103c8
framework = arduino
upload_protocol = stlink
debug_tool = stlink
pitfalls: "target voltage may be too low": the 3.3V wire isn't connected, or it's on the pin next to the 5V one
"init mode failed" / "unknown chip": most likely a clone chip, or the BOOT0 jumper isn't at 0
The pin labels on the aluminum shell are the ones to trust; diagrams online differ from vendor to vendor
parts.note: A must for the Blue Pill; also lets you single-step debug in PlatformIO

parts.name: USB to TTL serial adapter (CH340)
parts.volt: Jumper selects 3.3V / 5V; set it to 3.3V for the Blue Pill
parts.buy: CH340 USB to TTL serial adapter module
parts.pins: 3V3 5V TXD RXD GND
parts.wiring: Module TXD→Blue Pill PA10(RX1), module RXD→PA9(TX1), GND to GND (common ground). Remember: TX goes to RX, they cross
pitfalls: Not receiving a single character: first suspect TX/RX aren't crossed, then suspect a missing common ground
A screen full of question marks or garbage: baud rates don't match on the two sides; use pio device monitor -b 115200
Recent macOS versions include a CH340 driver; older systems need the CH34x driver installed
parts.note: A must for viewing serial output; it's your "eyes" while coding

parts.name: Digital multimeter (entry level)
parts.buy: digital multimeter auto-ranging beginner
parts.pins: Red probe in VΩmA, black probe in COM
parts.wiring: Measuring voltage: set to DC V, black probe on GND, red probe on the pin to measure, in parallel with the circuit. Checking continuity: set to the beep/diode range, touch the two points; a beep means connected
pitfalls: Never measure voltage with the dial on the current (A) range; that's a short circuit and will blow the fuse
Power off before checking continuity, otherwise readings are garbage and you may damage the meter
Measure first, ask later; it saves an hour
parts.note: The first time something "does nothing", this is what saves you

parts.name: Temperature-controlled soldering iron (T12 / 936 style)
parts.buy: T12 soldering station kit
parts.wiring: Soldering headers onto a module: stick the header into a breadboard to hold it, set the module on top, touch the iron tip to both the pad and the pin for 1 second, feed solder, pull the solder away first, then the iron
parts.snippet:
// No code needed. Temperature 320-350°C, 2-3 seconds per joint.
// Afterwards, use the multimeter's continuity range to check that neighboring pins aren't bridged.
pitfalls: Many sensor modules ship without headers soldered; if you can't solder, buy the "headers pre-soldered" version
Buy rosin-core solder wire, otherwise nothing will stick and you'll question your life choices
A shiny ball of solder after soldering is a cold joint; reheat it
parts.note: You'll need this sooner or later. Get a temperature-controlled one; the cheap unregulated irons are painful to use

parts.name: USB logic analyzer (24MHz, 8 channels)
parts.buy: USB logic analyzer 24MHz 8 channel
parts.pins: CH0-CH7 GND
parts.wiring: Clip CH0 to Blue Pill PB6(SCL), CH1 to PB7(SDA), GND to common ground; add the I2C decoder in PulseView and you'll see every byte and address
parts.snippet:
// No code needed. PulseView: pick fx2lafw as the device, set the sample rate to 4x or more of the signal frequency,
// add a Protocol Decoder: I2C / UART / SPI, and read the protocol contents directly.
pitfalls: When I2C/SPI/serial "doesn't work", this is a hundred times more useful than a multimeter: you can see exactly what was sent
The sample rate must be at least 4x the signal frequency; any less and you'll see garbage
It only sees 0s and 1s; for analog waveforms you need an oscilloscope
parts.note: The go-to tool for debugging communication problems; cheaper and handier than an oscilloscope

parts.name: Wire stripper + flush cutters + needle-nose pliers set
parts.buy: wire stripper flush cutter needle nose pliers electronics tool set
parts.wiring: Stripping: pick the notch matching the wire gauge, clamp the insulation, twist half a turn and pull. Use the flush cutters to cut header strips and trim excess leads
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: Don't strip insulation with your teeth or with scissors; if you nick through half the copper strands, the connection will be flaky
parts.note: You can skip these during the breadboard phase, but once you start wiring and soldering yourself they're indispensable

parts.name: USB voltage/current meter
parts.buy: USB voltage current meter tester
parts.pins: USB male in, USB female out
parts.wiring: Plug it in between your computer/charger and the board; it shows in real time how much current the board is drawing
parts.snippet:
// No code needed. Reference: a Blue Pill idles at about 30-40mA,
// one SG90 servo draws 200-700mA while moving, each WS2812 at full white draws 60mA.
pitfalls: A computer USB port typically supplies only 500mA; exceed it and it cuts power and the board reboots. When you see current approaching 0.5A, it's time for a separate power supply
parts.note: The most direct way to answer "do I need a separate power supply?"

parts.name: Soldering consumables: solder wire + flux + desoldering pump + tip cleaner
parts.buy: 0.8mm rosin core solder wire flux desoldering pump kit
parts.wiring: Made a mistake: heat the joint with the iron, aim the desoldering pump at it and press; it sucks the solder away
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: 0.8mm solder wire is the most versatile; thicker wire tends to bridge header pins
Wipe off rosin residue with alcohol after soldering, otherwise it stays sticky
parts.note: Buy together with the soldering iron

parts.name: Resistor kit (1/4W, 20 of each common value)
parts.buy: resistor kit 1/4W through-hole assortment common values
parts.pins: Two leads, no polarity
parts.wiring: LED current limiting: 3.3V→220Ω→LED long leg, LED short leg→GND. Pull-up: 3.3V→10kΩ→signal line. I2C pull-ups: 4.7kΩ from each of SCL and SDA to 3.3V
pitfalls: Can't read the color bands? Just measure with the multimeter's Ω range instead of memorizing them
Don't use 1/4W resistors as high-current dividers or loads; they'll get hot
parts.note: Must-buy. 220Ω for current limiting, 10kΩ pull-ups, 4.7kΩ I2C pull-ups

parts.name: 1N5819 Schottky diode (flyback / kickback protection)
parts.volt: 40V 1A, good for small pumps, small motors, relay coils
parts.buy: 1N5819 Schottky diode through-hole pack
parts.pins: The end with the white/gray band is the negative side (cathode)
parts.wiring: Connect in reverse parallel across the pump/motor: banded end to motor positive (+), unbanded end to motor negative. In normal operation no current flows through it; the instant power is cut, the motor's kickback current loops back through it instead of destroying the MOSFET
pitfalls: Reversed, it's a dead short across the supply and heats up the moment you power on
Most MOSFET modules and motor driver boards already include this protection, so you may not need to buy it separately
parts.note: If your MOSFET module already has flyback protection, no need to buy separately

parts.name: 1000μF 10V/16V electrolytic capacitor
parts.volt: Voltage rating should be one step above the supply: use 10V or 16V for a 5V circuit
parts.buy: 1000uF 16V electrolytic capacitor through-hole pack
parts.pins: Long leg is positive; the side with the white stripe is negative
parts.wiring: Connect across the servo/motor's 5V and GND, as close to the load as possible. It's like a small water tower: when the servo jerks, the voltage doesn't collapse and reboot the board
parts.snippet:
// No code needed.
// Symptom: the board reboots / serial turns to garbage whenever the servo moves → add this.
pitfalls: Reversed polarity makes it bulge or even burst; the white stripe side is negative
Don't pick a voltage rating equal to the supply voltage; for a 5V circuit buy 10V or higher
parts.note: Connect across 5V and GND near the servo; mind the polarity

parts.name: Ceramic capacitor kit (104 = 0.1μF etc.)
parts.buy: ceramic capacitor kit through-hole assortment 104
parts.pins: Two leads, no polarity
parts.wiring: Put a 104 across the VCC and GND pins of every chip/module to soak up high-frequency noise on the supply; put one across a button for hardware debouncing
pitfalls: Unlike electrolytic caps, these have no polarity
Their job is "stability"; most circuits run without them, but when something reboots or crashes mysteriously, think of them first
parts.note: Use with electrolytics: the electrolytic handles big swings, the ceramic handles small spikes

parts.name: Electrolytic capacitor kit (1μF-1000μF assortment)
parts.buy: electrolytic capacitor kit through-hole assortment
parts.pins: Long leg positive, white stripe side negative
parts.wiring: Put 10-100μF across the power input and output, next to motors, and at the LDO output, and the voltage settles down
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: Don't reverse the polarity
Cheap no-name caps often have inflated capacity ratings; in critical spots (motor power) go one size up
parts.note: For power filtering, like a reservoir

parts.name: 1N4007 rectifier diode
parts.buy: 1N4007 rectifier diode through-hole pack
parts.pins: The banded end is the negative side (cathode)
parts.wiring: In series on the positive supply line for reverse-polarity protection: banded end toward the load. Or as a flyback diode across a relay coil: banded end to the coil's supply positive
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: It eats 0.7V; put it in series in a 3.3V circuit and you're left with 2.6V, so don't
For fast switching (PWM motors) use a 1N5819 Schottky; this one is slow to respond
parts.note: Reverse-polarity protection and relay flyback, a few cents of insurance

parts.name: S8050 NPN transistor (TO-92)
parts.buy: S8050 NPN transistor TO-92 pack
parts.pins: Facing the flat printed side, left to right: E B C
parts.wiring: Blue Pill PB0→1kΩ→B (base); E (emitter)→GND; the load (buzzer/small lamp) goes between 5V and C (collector). Think of a faucet: a small GPIO current opens the valve, a big load current flows through
pitfalls: Always put a resistor (around 1kΩ) in series with the base; connecting it straight to a GPIO will burn the transistor or the pin
Above 500mA of load, don't use this; switch to a MOSFET
Different part numbers have different E B C orders; check the pinout when you swap types
parts.note: For small things a GPIO can't drive directly (big buzzers, small fans, several LEDs), let this do the heavy lifting

parts.name: Transistor kit (S8050/S8550/2N2222/2N3906 assortment)
parts.buy: transistor assortment kit TO-92 NPN PNP through-hole
parts.pins: E B C order differs by part number; check the packaging/datasheet
parts.wiring: NPN (S8050/2N2222) as a low-side switch: load between supply and C, E to GND. PNP (S8550) as a high-side switch: load between C and GND, E to supply
parts.snippet:
// NPN: GPIO HIGH turns it on
// PNP: GPIO LOW turns it on (note: the supply on the PNP's E must not exceed 3.3V, or the GPIO can't turn it off)
pitfalls: With a PNP's emitter on 5V, a 3.3V GPIO can't pull high enough and the transistor won't turn off. On a Blue Pill, either run the PNP from 3.3V or add an NPN stage in front
parts.note: A single S8050 is enough; this kit is for having spares

parts.name: 8MHz crystal + 32.768kHz watch crystal
parts.buy: 8MHz crystal HC-49S through-hole
parts.pins: Two leads, no polarity
parts.wiring: Only needed if you design your own PCB: the crystal's two leads go to OSC_IN/OSC_OUT, each with a 20pF capacitor to GND. The Blue Pill already has one soldered on
parts.snippet: // No code needed. The crystal is the chip's "metronome"; 8MHz is multiplied internally to 72MHz.
pitfalls: Blue Pill/Black Pill users don't need to buy this; it's on the board
Knock the onboard crystal off and the whole board won't start; on a board that's been dropped, check it first
parts.note: Just know what it does; only buy it if you design your own board

parts.name: PC817 optocoupler
parts.buy: PC817 optocoupler DIP-4 pack
parts.pins: 1 anode(+) 2 cathode(-) 3 emitter 4 collector (the dot/beveled corner marks pin 1)
parts.wiring: Blue Pill PB0→330Ω→pin 1, pin 2→GND. Far-side circuit: pin 3→far-side GND, pin 4→far-side signal line (with a 10kΩ pull-up to the far-side supply). The two sides talk only via light; no electrical connection
pitfalls: The output side only passes tens of mA; it carries signals, it doesn't switch loads
The output is inverted: input LED on, output pin pulled low
Never tie the two grounds together; that defeats the whole point of isolation
parts.note: Isolates two circuits with different voltages or grounds, e.g. controlling 12V gear or two boards at different voltages

parts.name: ULN2003 Darlington array (DIP-16 chip)
parts.volt: Drives from 3.3V inputs; output side up to 50V, 500mA per channel
parts.buy: ULN2003APG DIP-16 through-hole pack
parts.wiring: Blue Pill PB0-PB3→IN1-4; load between supply positive and OUT; COM to the load's supply positive (for relays/motor coils); pin 8 GND shares a common ground with the Blue Pill
pitfalls: It's a low-side switch: the load sits between supply positive and OUT, and OUT is the end that gets connected to GND
Keep total current per chip under about 1A; all 7 channels at a full 500mA gets too hot to touch
parts.note: This is the chip on the green board that comes with the 28BYJ-48 stepper. Seven low-power switches; one chip replaces seven transistors

parts.name: Resettable fuse (PTC 0.5A-2A)
parts.buy: PTC resettable fuse through-hole 1A pack
parts.pins: Two leads, no polarity
parts.wiring: In series on the 5V positive line feeding the module. When current exceeds the rating it heats up, goes high-resistance and opens; once it cools it resets by itself
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: Slow to react (hundreds of ms); it protects against burnt wires and boards, not against instantly frying a chip
Computer USB ports have their own protection; you only need this when powering from an adapter or battery
parts.note: An escape hatch when powering from a battery or a beefy adapter

parts.name: Breadboard (half-size, 400 tie points)
parts.buy: solderless breadboard 400 tie points
parts.pins: Each vertical column of 5 holes in the middle is connected; the power rails along the top and bottom run horizontally
parts.wiring: Straddle the Blue Pill across the center gap so each row of pins lands on one side; run one wire each from 3.3V and GND to the power rails, then take every module's VCC/GND from the rails
parts.snippet:
// No code needed.
// Two things to remember: 5 holes in a vertical column are one group; a horizontal power rail is one group along its whole length.
pitfalls: On some breadboards the power rail is split in the middle, so half the rail is live and half isn't; confirm with the multimeter's continuity range
Forcing in oversized leads (big capacitors, power adapter wires) stretches the holes and causes flaky contacts later
If a module on the breadboard isn't connecting, pull it out and reseat it first
parts.note: 5 holes in a vertical column are connected; power rails run horizontally

parts.name: Breadboard (full-size, 830 tie points)
parts.buy: solderless breadboard 830 tie points with power rails
parts.pins: 2 power rails on each side
parts.wiring: Same as the 400, just twice as long; fits a Blue Pill + a display + three or four modules at once
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: The rails on the two sides are independent; 3.3V on the left doesn't automatically appear on the right, so jumper them across
parts.note: Switch to this once a project grows, or buy two 400s and snap them together

parts.name: Jumper wires (male-female / male-male / female-female, one strip each)
parts.buy: jumper wires 40 pin 20cm male-female male-male female-female
parts.wiring: Male-male: breadboard hole to hole; male-female: breadboard to module header pins; female-female: module header pins to Blue Pill header pins
parts.snippet:
// No code needed.
// Color convention: red = power, black = GND, anything else is up to you; sticking to it saves a lot of debugging time.
pitfalls: Peel the ribbon into single wires; the whole strip will not plug in
Jumper wires are the most common failure point: bad contact, or broken inside. When in doubt, swap the wire
20cm is plenty; overly long wires get flaky on I2C/SPI
parts.note: One strip of each of the three types, red and black clearly marked
parts.identify: How to identify: kit jumper wires come as a 40-wire rainbow ribbon stuck together. Peel off as many single wires as you need from the edge (normal, it does not damage them). Ends: a black plastic sleeve is a female end (goes over a pin); a bare metal pin is a male end (goes into a hole). The female sleeve shows a tiny metal dot on one side: that is the latch of the crimp inside. There is no right way up; slide it fully onto the pin either way.

parts.name: Header pins / female headers (2.54mm, 40-pin)
parts.buy: 2.54mm single row header pins female headers 40 pin
parts.wiring: Solder them onto modules that come without pins; solder female headers if you want the Blue Pill to be removable
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: Snap off the number of pins you need with flush cutters; you'll sacrifice one pin at the break
Female headers are harder to solder than male; practice on male ones first
parts.note: Buy together with the soldering iron

parts.name: Plastic waterproof enclosure / acrylic case
parts.buy: waterproof plastic junction box electronics enclosure DIY
parts.wiring: Stick the breadboard to the bottom of the box with double-sided tape; seal the cable opening with hot glue
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: Measure the breadboard plus modules before buying, and leave an extra 1cm
Sensors (temperature/humidity, light) need to be exposed outside the box to read accurately
parts.note: Only needed once a finished project is going on a windowsill or balcony

parts.name: M3 screw, nut and brass standoff kit
parts.buy: M3 screws nuts brass standoffs nylon standoffs assortment kit box
parts.wiring: The holes at the corners of most boards are M3 (3mm); standoffs lift the board so the back doesn't touch metal and short
parts.snippet: // No code needed.
pitfalls: The Blue Pill has no mounting holes; to fix it in place, use the breadboard or hot glue
Nylon standoffs don't conduct; with metal standoffs make sure they don't touch solder joints on the back of the board
parts.note: For mounting enclosures and fixing servos

parts.name: Tactile push button 6x6 (4-pin)
parts.buy: 6x6x5mm tactile push button switch through-hole pack
parts.pins: 4 pins: the two on the same side are already connected; pressing connects the diagonal pair
parts.wiring: One pin to Blue Pill PB0, the diagonally opposite pin to GND; use INPUT_PULLUP in code, no external resistor needed. Not pressed = HIGH, pressed = LOW
pitfalls: One press counts several times: mechanical bounce; after a press, delay(20-50) and read again, or track time with millis
It reads "connected" no matter how you plug it into the breadboard: you're using the two pins on the same side; switch to the diagonal pair
Pressed is LOW, not HIGH; the logic is inverted in pull-up mode
parts.note: Wire the diagonal pair. Needs debouncing

parts.name: Potentiometer 10kΩ (knob module)
parts.buy: 10K potentiometer module knob
parts.pins: VCC GND OUT (or + - S)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, OUT→PA0. It's like a faucet: wherever you turn it, PA0 reads that much
pitfalls: Don't put 5V across the ends; the wiper would exceed 3.3V and damage the ADC pin
Readings jump near the ends: the knob isn't linear near its limits, so leave some margin
STM32duino's analogRead defaults to 10-bit 0-1023; for 0-4095 add analogReadResolution(12)
parts.note: The most intuitive input for brightness, speed, and menu selection

parts.name: VS1838B IR receiver + remote control kit
parts.buy: IR remote control kit VS1838B receiver remote
parts.pins: Receiver: OUT GND VCC (left to right facing the lens; module version is S - +)
parts.wiring: OUT→Blue Pill PB8, VCC→3.3V, GND→GND. Point the remote at it and press; the key codes print to serial
pitfalls: The IRremote 3.x/4.x API is completely different from older online tutorials (2.x); the header is IRremote.hpp
Every remote has different key codes; print them out first, then write your if statements
Fluorescent lights and direct sunlight interfere; getting a bunch of garbage codes is normal
parts.note: Control your stuff with any remote in the house

parts.name: KY-040 rotary encoder module (with push button)
parts.buy: KY-040 rotary encoder module
parts.lib: attachInterrupt (read the A/B phases in an interrupt)
parts.pins: CLK DT SW + GND
parts.wiring: CLK→PB8, DT→PB9, SW→PB5, +→3.3V, GND→GND. Each click changes CLK and DT one after the other; which changes first tells you the direction
pitfalls: Polling in loop misses clicks; interrupts overcount because of bounce. Cheap encoders are bouncy by nature; counting on only one edge of CLK helps a lot
One click counts as 2 or 4: that's normal, just divide
The SW button reads LOW when pressed
parts.note: A menu knob: turn and press in one part

parts.name: 4x4 membrane matrix keypad
parts.buy: 4x4 membrane matrix keypad 16 key
parts.pins: 8 wires: R1-R4 (rows) C1-C4 (columns), left to right
parts.wiring: R1-R4→PB12 PB13 PB14 PB15, C1-C4→PA8 PA11 PA12 PA15. The library powers each row in turn and watches which column responds, scanning 16 keys with 8 wires
pitfalls: Press 1 and get 4: rows and columns are swapped; swap the rows and cols arrays
The ribbon connector has no soldered pins; use male-female jumper wires to get it onto a breadboard
parts.note: Combination lock project

parts.name: Dual-axis PS2 joystick module
parts.buy: PS2 dual axis joystick module with button
parts.pins: GND +5V VRx VRy SW
parts.wiring: Connect the +5V pin to the Blue Pill's 3.3V (NOT 5V!), VRx→PA0, VRy→PA1, SW→PB5 (INPUT_PULLUP), GND→GND
pitfalls: The silkscreen says +5V, but on a Blue Pill feed it 3.3V or the ADC pins get overvoltage
At rest it's not exactly the center value (512); add a ±50 dead zone
The SW button needs a pull-up and reads LOW when pressed
parts.note: Robot car remote, game controller

parts.name: TTP223 capacitive touch button
parts.buy: TTP223 capacitive touch sensor module pack
parts.pins: VCC GND SIG (or I/O)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SIG→PB0. Touch it with a finger and SIG goes HIGH; it even senses through 2mm of plastic
pitfalls: Two solder jumpers on the back: A changes the default level, B switches toggle/momentary; default is momentary, active-high
Don't touch it while powering up; it self-calibrates at boot
Plastic enclosures are fine, metal panels are not
parts.note: For panels without mechanical buttons

parts.name: Slide switch / rocker switch
parts.buy: SS12D00 slide switch 3 pin through-hole pack
parts.pins: 3 pins: the middle is common; it connects to whichever side you slide toward
parts.wiring: As an input: middle pin→PB0 (INPUT_PULLUP), one side pin→GND. As a power switch: in series on the battery's positive line
pitfalls: Small slide switches only handle a few hundred mA; don't run motor power through them
Rocker switch pins aren't on 2.54mm spacing and won't fit a breadboard; solder wires to them
parts.note: Main power switch or mode selector

parts.name: SW-520D ball tilt switch
parts.buy: SW-520D ball tilt switch sensor module
parts.pins: Two pins (module version: VCC GND DO)
parts.wiring: One pin→PB0 (INPUT_PULLUP), the other→GND. There's a small steel ball inside: upright it conducts, tipped over it opens
pitfalls: It only tells you whether it tipped over; for how many degrees you need an MPU6050
The ball rattles, so reading a string of 0101 is normal; read several times and take the majority
parts.note: The cheapest "did it get knocked over" detector

parts.name: Reed switch (magnetic switch) + small magnet
parts.buy: reed switch normally open 2x14mm magnetic switch module
parts.pins: Two pins (module version: VCC GND DO)
parts.wiring: One pin→PB0 (INPUT_PULLUP), the other→GND. Bring a magnet close and the two reeds inside the glass tube pull together and conduct
pitfalls: The glass tube is fragile; hold the lead at its base with tweezers when bending it
Sensing range is only about 1cm, so mount the magnet close
parts.note: Door/window open detection: magnet on the door, reed switch on the frame

parts.name: Micro switch / limit switch (with roller lever)
parts.buy: KW11-3Z micro limit switch roller lever
parts.pins: COM NO NC, 3 pins
parts.wiring: COM→PB0 (INPUT_PULLUP), NO→GND. Pressed: COM connects to NO (LOW); released: COM connects to NC
pitfalls: Don't mix up NO (normally open) and NC (normally closed); wiring NC makes it "LOW when not touched"
Needs debouncing too
parts.note: Stops a motor automatically at the end of travel; 3D printers and linear slides depend on it

parts.name: 12mm latching/momentary push button (with LED)
parts.volt: Switch is passive; LED 3-5V, needs a current-limiting resistor
parts.buy: 12mm metal push button switch with LED latching momentary
parts.pins: 5 pins: C NO NC for the switch, + - for the LED
parts.wiring: C→PB0 (INPUT_PULLUP), NO→GND; LED +→220Ω→PB1, LED -→GND
pitfalls: "Latching" clicks and stays down until pressed again; "momentary" pops back up when released. Decide before you buy
The panel needs a 12mm hole; on a plastic box use a step drill or a hot knife
parts.note: The big button on the enclosure panel

parts.name: 0.96-inch OLED SSD1306 (I2C, 4-pin)
parts.buy: 0.96 inch OLED display I2C 4 pin SSD1306 (Adafruit carries an equivalent)
parts.pins: GND VCC SCL SDA
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7. Address is usually 0x3C
pitfalls: Blank screen: first run an I2C scanner sketch and look for 0x3C; if nothing shows, the wiring is wrong or VCC/GND are in a different order (some boards have GND as pin 1, others VCC)
Displaying Chinese needs a font like u8g2_font_wqy12_t_gb2312, which eats 100K+ of flash; the Blue Pill's 64K can't hold it, so use the _chinese1 subset
Yellow on top, blue on the bottom means it's a two-color panel, not a defect
parts.note: The most common small display; address 0x3C, the 4-pin version is the easiest

parts.name: 1.3-inch OLED SH1106 (I2C)
parts.buy: 1.3 inch OLED display I2C SH1106
parts.pins: GND VCC SCL SDA
parts.wiring: Same as the 0.96-inch: SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, VCC→3.3V. Just change the constructor to SH1106
pitfalls: Its driver chip differs from the 0.96-inch (SH1106 vs SSD1306); the wrong driver gives a shifted image or two missing columns on the right
1.3-inch panels also exist with SSD1306; check the silkscreen on the back when it arrives
parts.note: Same library as the 0.96-inch, just bigger text

parts.name: LCD1602 + I2C backpack (PCF8574)
parts.volt: 5V power (backlight and contrast need 5V); 3.3V I2C signals usually work fine
parts.buy: LCD1602 16x2 LCD display module I2C backpack blue or yellow-green (Adafruit/SparkFun carry an equivalent)
parts.pins: GND VCC SDA SCL
parts.wiring: VCC→Blue Pill 5V pin, GND→GND, SDA→PB7, SCL→PB6. PB6/PB7 are 5V-tolerant, so it's fine that the backpack pulls the bus up to 5V
pitfalls: Cannot find VCC/GND labels: the board prints VDD (= VCC); the labels sit next to the 4 pins on the display side, very small, so flip it over
Backlight on but no text: turn the blue trimmer pot on the back of the backpack to adjust contrast; turn until you see a row of blocks, then back off a little
Address is either 0x27 or 0x3F; run an I2C scanner
ASCII only, no Chinese or other non-Latin characters
parts.note: 2 rows x 16 characters, 5V power
parts.identify: How to identify: display side up, there is a row of 4 pins at one top corner. That is the connector. Silkscreen order is GND VDD SDA SCL (some boards print VCC): VDD is the same as VCC (power +), GND is the pin nearest the mounting hole. The 16 holes along the edge (VSS VDD V0 RS RW E D0-D7 A K) are the parallel interface and are left unconnected with I2C. Some kits build the I2C chip (PCF8574/HLF8574) straight onto the back of the display instead of a separate backpack; it works the same.
parts.wiring_esp32: ESP32: VDD(VCC)→5V pin (marked 5V/VIN), GND→GND, SDA→GPIO21, SCL→GPIO22. Use 4 female-female jumper wires (black sockets on both ends). On 3.3V the backlight is dim or off.

parts.name: LCD2004 + I2C backpack
parts.buy: LCD2004 20x4 LCD display module I2C blue backlight
parts.pins: GND VCC SDA SCL
parts.wiring: Same as LCD1602: VCC→5V, SDA→PB7, SCL→PB6
pitfalls: The third row in setCursor is (0, 2), not (0, 3); rows count from 0
Same as the 1602: adjust the contrast pot first
parts.note: 4 rows x 20 characters, plenty for a data readout panel

parts.name: 1.8" TFT color display ST7735 (SPI, 128x160)
parts.volt: 3.3V (some boards have an onboard LDO and accept 5V; check the silkscreen)
parts.buy: 1.8 inch TFT LCD display module SPI ST7735 128x160 (Adafruit carries an equivalent)
parts.pins: LED SCK SDA A0(DC) RESET CS GND VCC
parts.wiring: SCK→PA5, SDA(MOSI)→PA7, CS→PA4, A0/DC→PB0, RESET→PB1, LED→3.3V, VCC→3.3V, GND→GND
pitfalls: Wrong colors or shifted image: try INITR_GREENTAB / REDTAB as the initR argument; the factory tab color on the screen varies
lib_deps also needs adafruit/Adafruit GFX Library and adafruit/Adafruit BusIO
Garbled screen once you have lots of wires: jumper wires are too long; slow down SPI or use shorter wires
parts.note: Color; SPI needs 7-8 wires

parts.name: 1.3" IPS color display ST7789 (SPI, 240x240)
parts.buy: 1.3 inch IPS LCD display module ST7789 240x240 SPI
parts.pins: GND VCC SCL SDA RES DC BLK (some have no CS)
parts.wiring: SCL→PA5, SDA→PA7, DC→PB0, RES→PB1, BLK→3.3V (or a PWM pin for brightness), VCC→3.3V. If there's no CS pin, pass -1 in code
pitfalls: The version without a CS pin can't share the SPI bus with anything else (like an SD card)
Full 240x240 redraws are slow on an F103; only redraw the areas that changed
parts.note: IPS panel, colors look far better than the ST7735

parts.name: 2.8" TFT ILI9341 with touch (SPI, 320x240)
parts.buy: 2.8 inch TFT LCD display module ILI9341 SPI touch screen XPT2046
parts.pins: VCC GND CS RESET DC MOSI SCK LED MISO + touch T_CLK T_CS T_DIN T_DO T_IRQ
parts.wiring: SCK→PA5, MISO→PA6, MOSI→PA7, CS→PA4, DC→PB0, RESET→PB1, LED→3.3V. Touch T_CLK/T_DIN/T_DO share the same SPI lines, T_CS→PB10
pitfalls: The touch panel is a separate chip (XPT2046); add the paulstoffregen/XPT2046_Touchscreen library and calibrate it
The Blue Pill's 20K RAM can't hold a full-screen buffer, so animations flicker; for smooth graphics move to an F411/ESP32
On some boards the J1 jumper selects 3.3V/5V power; check the back
parts.note: The most common "touch screen" module; great for a small dashboard

parts.name: TM1637 4-digit 7-segment display module
parts.buy: TM1637 4-digit 7-segment LED display module clock
parts.pins: CLK DIO VCC GND
parts.wiring: CLK→PB8, DIO→PB9, VCC→3.3V, GND→GND. Any two GPIOs work; it doesn't use the I2C bus
pitfalls: It's not real I2C; don't hook it to PB6/PB7 and expect Wire to talk to it
Comes in 0.36" and 0.56" sizes; the version with a colon is good for clocks
parts.note: The easiest way to show temperature/time/counts, just two wires

parts.name: MAX7219 8x8 dot matrix (chainable, 4-in-1)
parts.buy: MAX7219 dot matrix module 8x8 4 in 1 LED display
parts.pins: VCC GND DIN CS CLK
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, DIN→PA7, CLK→PA5, CS→PA4. Chain multiple modules end to end: DOUT of one module to DIN of the next
pitfalls: Text mirrored or rotated 90 degrees: change the hardware type to FC16_HW / GENERIC_HW / PAROLA_HW and try again
lib_deps also needs majicdesigns/MD_MAX72XX
All four modules fully lit draw over 300mA; powering from the board's 3.3V will cause resets
parts.note: Scrolling text, little emoji faces

parts.name: 1.54" e-paper display (SPI, 200x200)
parts.buy: 1.54 inch e-paper e-ink display module SPI 200x200 (Waveshare or equivalent)
parts.pins: BUSY RST DC CS CLK DIN GND VCC
parts.wiring: CLK→PA5, DIN→PA7, CS→PA4, DC→PB0, RST→PB1, BUSY→PB10, VCC→3.3V, GND→GND
pitfalls: A refresh takes 2-3 seconds and flashes black/white a few times; that's normal, it isn't meant for animation
Several driver variants exist at this size (D67/GDEH0154 etc.); the model in the constructor must match the label on the back. lib_deps also needs adafruit/Adafruit GFX Library
Don't do frequent full refreshes; it shortens the panel's life. Call hibernate after drawing
parts.note: Keeps its image with power off; great for a desk weather sign or price tag

parts.name: Nokia 5110 LCD (PCD8544, 84x48)
parts.buy: Nokia 5110 LCD display module 84x48 blue backlight (Adafruit/SparkFun carry an equivalent)
parts.pins: RST CE DC DIN CLK VCC BL GND
parts.wiring: CLK→PA5, DIN→PA7, DC→PB0, CE→PA4, RST→PB1, VCC→3.3V, BL→3.3V through 220Ω, GND→GND
pitfalls: Text hard to read: try setContrast values from 40 to 70
The glass is held against the board by metal spring clips; if nothing shows, press down on the four corners first
parts.note: The old Nokia phone screen: low power, cheap, retro

parts.name: 5mm LEDs (red/yellow/green/blue assortment)
parts.volt: Red/yellow ~2V, green/blue/white ~3V; always use a series current-limiting resistor
parts.buy: 5mm LED assortment kit through hole red yellow green blue white
parts.pins: Long leg is + (anode), short leg is - (cathode, flat edge on the rim)
parts.wiring: PB0→220Ω→LED long leg, LED short leg→GND. For brightness control use a PWM pin (PB0 supports it)
pitfalls: No resistor: it flashes once and dies, or damages the GPIO pin
Doesn't light: flip it around first; nine times out of ten it's backwards
Blue/white LEDs are dimmer than red at 3.3V; that's normal
parts.note: Long leg is +. Use a 220Ω-1kΩ series resistor

parts.name: RGB LED (common cathode, 4-pin) / KY-016 module
parts.buy: RGB LED 5mm common cathode 4 pin / KY-016 RGB LED module
parts.pins: Longest leg is the common pin (common cathode goes to GND); the other three are R G B
parts.wiring: R→220Ω→PA6, G→220Ω→PA7, B→220Ω→PB0 (all PWM pins), longest leg→GND
pitfalls: Common-anode versions work backwards: 255 is off and 0 is full on, and the common pin goes to 3.3V
The three colors aren't equally bright; red being brighter is normal, so use a larger resistor on red
parts.note: For lots of individually addressable colors, use WS2812 instead

parts.name: WS2812B LED strip / LED ring / 8x8 LED matrix
parts.volt: 5V power; 3.3V data usually works, otherwise add a level shifter before the first LED
parts.buy: WS2812B LED ring 12 pixel / WS2812B LED strip 5V 60 LEDs per meter (Adafruit NeoPixel is the same part)
parts.pins: VCC(5V) GND DIN (plus DOUT to feed the next segment)
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, DIN→PB0. With more than 10 LEDs, get 5V from an external supply rather than the board's USB, but keep GND tied to the board (common ground)
pitfalls: Each LED at full white draws 60mA, so 60 LEDs is 3.6A; you need a separate 5V supply or the board will keep resetting
First LED dark or colors scrambled: the 3.3V signal is marginal; put 330Ω in series with DIN or add a 74HCT245 level shifter
Colors in the wrong order (red/green swapped): change GRB to RGB
parts.note: Every LED sets its own color. Over 10 LEDs needs its own 5V supply

parts.name: Active buzzer (beeps when powered)
parts.volt: 3.3V and 5V versions exist; buy the 3.3V one
parts.buy: active buzzer 3.3V through hole / active buzzer module Arduino
parts.pins: Long leg +, short leg - (+ is marked on top)
parts.wiring: +→PB0, -→GND. It has a built-in oscillator, so a HIGH level makes it play one fixed tone
pitfalls: Active and passive buzzers look identical; the active one has a sticker on top and black epoxy on the back, while the passive one shows a green circuit board
Some module versions are active-low (sound only when you write LOW)
Loud ones (>30mA) need a transistor to drive them
parts.note: One tone as soon as it gets power; the simplest alarm

parts.name: Passive buzzer (can play melodies)
parts.buy: passive buzzer module through hole Arduino piezo
parts.pins: + - (or VCC GND I/O)
parts.wiring: +→PB0, -→GND. It works like a tiny speaker: whatever frequency you feed it is the pitch you hear
pitfalls: digitalWrite(HIGH) just gives a single click; use tone()
tone uses a hardware timer and may conflict with Servo/PWM; try a different pin
parts.note: Plays melodies. Don't confuse it with the active buzzer

parts.name: Coin vibration motor (phone-style)
parts.buy: coin vibration motor 1027 3V flat mini DC vibrating motor
parts.pins: Red + blue/black -
parts.wiring: Don't drive it straight from a GPIO: PB0→1kΩ→S8050 base, emitter→GND, motor red wire→3.3V, blue wire→S8050 collector; put a 1N5819 diode across the motor in reverse
pitfalls: A GPIO can only supply about 20mA; wired directly, the motor won't spin at best and burns out the pin at worst
Module versions (with a transistor onboard) can go straight to a GPIO; bare motors need your own transistor
parts.note: For wristbands and reminder gadgets

parts.name: KY-008 laser module (red, 650nm)
parts.buy: KY-008 laser transmitter module 650nm red dot Arduino
parts.pins: S (signal), middle pin, - (GND)
parts.wiring: S→PB0, -→GND (the middle pin is VCC on some boards and unconnected on others; check the silkscreen). Pair it with a photoresistor for a "laser tripwire alarm"
pitfalls: Never look into it or point it at anyone's eyes, especially kids
30mA is close to the GPIO limit; for long-term use drive it through a transistor
parts.note: Laser tripwire alarm, cat toy

parts.name: PAM8403 amplifier board + small speaker (3W 8Ω)
parts.buy: PAM8403 mini amplifier board 5V + 4 ohm 3W small speaker
parts.pins: +5V GND L R GND(audio) L+ L- R+ R-
parts.wiring: +5V→5V, GND→GND; Blue Pill PB0 (PWM)→10kΩ→L input, L+ L-→speaker; on the version with a volume pot, set it halfway
pitfalls: Feeding raw PWM in only gives square-wave "electronic" beeps; for music you need a DFPlayer or a DAC
On boards with separate audio GND and power GND, connect both
Long speaker wires or wires near a motor will hum
parts.note: For real sound, use a DFPlayer instead

parts.name: DFPlayer Mini MP3 player module
parts.buy: DFPlayer Mini MP3 player module microSD TF card Arduino (DFRobot makes the original)
parts.pins: VCC RX TX SPK_1 GND SPK_2 DAC_R DAC_L
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, module RX←Blue Pill PA2 (TX2) through 1kΩ, module TX→PA3 (RX2); SPK_1/SPK_2 drive an 8Ω speaker directly. On the microSD card, create an mp3 folder and put 0001.mp3 in it
pitfalls: The microSD card must be FAT32, filenames must be four digits like 0001.mp3, and they go in the mp3 folder
Noise or hissing: put 1kΩ in series with the RX line and add a 100μF capacitor on the power
Clone chips have slightly different commands; if begin fails, try isACK=false
parts.note: Voice prompts, doorbells, music boxes

parts.name: 12V single-color LED strip (5050/2835)
parts.buy: 12V LED strip 5050 warm white 5m roll
parts.pins: +12V - (GND)
parts.wiring: 12V adapter +→strip +; strip -→MOSFET module V-; MOSFET module SIG→Blue Pill PB0 (PWM), MOSFET module GND and Blue Pill GND tied together (common ground)
pitfalls: 12V must never touch any Blue Pill pin; the two sides share only GND
The strip is made of 3-LED segments; only cut at the marked cut lines (scissor symbol)
A low PWM frequency gives visible flicker; raise it with analogWriteFrequency(1000)
parts.note: Mood lighting, desk lights; cheaper and simpler than WS2812 when you don't need color changes

parts.name: Photoresistor (LDR) 5528 (or KY-018 module)
parts.buy: photoresistor LDR 5528 GL5528 pack / KY-018 photoresistor module
parts.pins: Two legs, no polarity (module version: VCC GND AO)
parts.wiring: Bare part: 3.3V→photoresistor→PA0, PA0→10kΩ→GND, read the divider voltage on PA0. Brighter light means lower resistance and a higher reading
pitfalls: Wiring one leg to 3.3V and the other straight to the ADC gives no change; it must form a voltage divider with a fixed resistor
The reading is relative, not illuminance; for lux values use a BH1750
Batches vary a lot, so measure and set your own thresholds
parts.note: Divider with 10kΩ, read on ADC; makes a light-activated lamp

parts.name: BH1750 ambient light sensor GY-302
parts.buy: BH1750 GY-302 digital light intensity sensor module lux I2C (Adafruit carries an equivalent)
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA ADDR
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, leave ADDR unconnected (address 0x23)
pitfalls: Readings like -1 or 54612: I2C isn't talking; run an address scan
Tying ADDR to 3.3V changes the address to 0x5C, so two modules can coexist
parts.note: Gives lux directly: indoors 100-500, tens of thousands in sunlight

parts.name: DHT11 temperature & humidity module
parts.buy: DHT11 temperature humidity sensor module 3 pin Arduino
parts.pins: VCC DATA GND (3-pin module; on the 4-pin bare sensor the middle pin is unused and DATA needs a 10kΩ pull-up)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, DATA→PB8
pitfalls: Reading nan: wiring is wrong, less than 1 second since power-on, or reading too fast (wait at least 1-2 seconds between reads)
lib_deps also needs adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor
Accuracy is ±2°C ±5%RH, fine for watching trends
parts.note: Modest accuracy, fine for starting out. Upgrade to DHT22 or SHT30

parts.name: DHT22 / AM2302 temperature & humidity module
parts.buy: DHT22 AM2302 temperature humidity sensor module (Adafruit/SparkFun carry an equivalent)
parts.pins: VCC DATA GND
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, DATA→PB8, exactly the same as the DHT11
pitfalls: Same library as the DHT11; just change DHT11 to DHT22. With the wrong type the readings are all garbage
Wait at least 2 seconds between reads
parts.note: More accurate than the DHT11 (±0.5°C), same library

parts.name: SHT30 temperature & humidity module (I2C)
parts.volt: 3.3V (some modules have an LDO and accept 5V)
parts.buy: SHT30 temperature humidity sensor module I2C
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA (some also have ADR)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, address 0x44
pitfalls: Pulling the ADR pin high changes the address to 0x45
Don't mount it right next to anything warm (a voltage regulator, a display); it will read 2-3 degrees high
parts.note: Industrial-grade accuracy, two wires; SHT30/31/35 share one library

parts.name: DS18B20 waterproof temperature probe
parts.buy: DS18B20 waterproof temperature sensor probe stainless steel 1m 3 pack
parts.pins: Red VCC, black/blue GND, yellow DATA
parts.wiring: Red→3.3V, black→GND, yellow→PB8, plus a 4.7kΩ pull-up between the yellow wire and 3.3V (without it you read -127)
pitfalls: Reading -127 or 85: missing pull-up resistor, wrong wiring, or a counterfeit chip
lib_deps also needs paulstoffregen/OneWire
Several probes can share one wire; read the second one with getTempCByIndex(1)
parts.note: Can sit in water to measure temperature. Data line needs a 4.7kΩ pull-up

parts.name: NTC thermistor 10kΩ (B=3950)
parts.buy: NTC thermistor 10K 3950 waterproof probe pack
parts.pins: Two legs, no polarity
parts.wiring: 3.3V→10kΩ fixed resistor→PA0, PA0→NTC→GND. Higher temperature means lower NTC resistance and a lower reading on PA0
pitfalls: The 10000 and 3950 in the formula must match the part you bought; the wrong type puts you off by 10+ degrees
Accuracy depends on that fixed resistor; use a 1% one
parts.note: The cheapest way to measure temperature; 3D printer heated beds use exactly this

parts.name: MAX6675 K-type thermocouple module (high temperatures)
parts.buy: MAX6675 K-type thermocouple temperature sensor module 0-1024C with probe
parts.pins: GND VCC SCK CS SO + the two thermocouple wires
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCK→PA5, SO→PA6, CS→PA4; thermocouple red wire to -, blue/yellow wire to + (reversed, the temperature runs backwards)
pitfalls: With the thermocouple reversed, the reading drops as things heat up
Reading nan: thermocouple not seated properly, or reading too fast
0.25°C resolution and so-so accuracy at room temperature; it's meant for 100°C and up
parts.note: Ovens, coffee roasting, soldering iron tips; the DS18B20 tops out at 125°C, this goes to 1000°C

parts.name: MLX90614 non-contact infrared thermometer GY-906
parts.volt: 3.3V (the GY-906 module has an LDO and accepts 5V)
parts.buy: MLX90614 GY-906 non-contact infrared temperature sensor module I2C (Adafruit/SparkFun carry an equivalent)
parts.pins: VIN GND SCL SDA
parts.wiring: VIN→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, address 0x5A
pitfalls: It measures the average temperature of everything in its field of view; from farther away the background gets averaged in, so measure foreheads within 3cm
Suffixes like BAA (90° field of view) and DCI (5° narrow field) exist; pick the narrow one for distant targets
parts.note: Measures temperature without touching; this is the chip inside forehead thermometers

parts.name: Soil moisture sensor (capacitive v1.2/v2.0)
parts.volt: 3.3-5V (powered at 3.3V the output stays under 3.3V, which is safe)
parts.buy: capacitive soil moisture sensor v1.2 corrosion resistant analog
parts.pins: VCC GND AOUT
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, AOUT→PA0. Push it into the soil leaving the circuit-board part exposed; dry soil reads high, wet soil reads low
pitfalls: Buy the capacitive type, not the resistive one (the two-prong fork); resistive ones corrode away after a few weeks
You must calibrate the dry/wet endpoints yourself: take one reading in air and one in water
The circuit-board part must stay dry; insert only up to the white line
parts.note: The heart of any plant-watering project. Buy capacitive

parts.name: Water level sensor (interdigitated traces)
parts.buy: water level sensor liquid level detection module Arduino
parts.wiring: +→PB1 (power it from a GPIO: only turn it on while measuring and off otherwise, to prevent corrosion), -→GND, S→PA0. The more of it is underwater, the higher the reading
pitfalls: Left powered in water it corrodes electrolytically within weeks; use a GPIO as its power and only turn it on to measure
Only gives a rough more/less water reading; for an accurate height use ultrasonic or a pressure sensor
parts.note: Warns you when the tank is running low

parts.name: Rain sensor (with comparator board)
parts.buy: rain drop sensor module raindrop detection with comparator board Arduino
parts.pins: Sensing plate has two pins that go to the small board; small board has VCC GND DO AO
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, AO→PA0 (wetter = lower reading), DO→PB0 (goes LOW past the threshold; set the threshold with the pot on the small board)
pitfalls: The sensing plate corrodes if it sits wet for long; like the water level sensor, power it only while measuring
DO means "rain = LOW"; don't test for HIGH
parts.note: Laundry reminder, automatic awning

parts.name: YF-S201 water flow sensor (Hall effect)
parts.volt: 5V power, 5V output pulses → use 5V-tolerant pin PB8 or a voltage divider
parts.buy: YF-S201 water flow sensor Hall effect flowmeter G1/2
parts.pins: Red VCC, black GND, yellow signal
parts.wiring: Red→5V, black→GND, yellow→PB8 (PB8 is 5V-tolerant). Inside is a little turbine that emits a few pulses per turn; count the pulses to get flow
pitfalls: The signal is 5V; don't connect it to PA0-PA7, which aren't 5V-tolerant
At very low flow the turbine doesn't spin, so 0 doesn't mean no water
The fitting is G1/2 thread; buy adapters for your tubing
parts.note: Logs how much water your plant-watering system used

parts.name: HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor
parts.volt: 5V power; Echo outputs 5V, so on the Blue Pill use a voltage divider or a 5V-tolerant pin
parts.buy: HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor module Arduino 5 pack
parts.pins: VCC Trig Echo GND
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, Trig→PB0, Echo→PB8 (PB8 is 5V-tolerant; on a PA pin use a 1kΩ+2kΩ divider). Works like a bat: send a chirp, listen for the echo, time it
pitfalls: Barely works at 3.3V; it needs 5V
Reads 0 or jumps around: Echo is miswired, or nothing is in front of it within 4 meters
Soft or angled surfaces (fabric, a sloped couch) return weak echoes; bad readings there are the sensor's fault, not yours
parts.note: 5V device; the Echo pin needs a divider or a 5V-tolerant STM32 pin

parts.name: VL53L0X laser distance sensor (ToF)
parts.buy: VL53L0X time of flight laser distance sensor module GY-530 (Adafruit/Pololu carry an equivalent)
parts.pins: VIN GND SCL SDA XSHUT GPIO1
parts.wiring: VIN→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, address 0x29
pitfalls: Range is only up to 2 meters, less in direct sunlight
Every module ships at address 0x29; to use several, power them up one at a time via XSHUT and change the address
There's a protective film from the factory; peel it off
parts.note: More precise than ultrasonic, tiny, fine with soft surfaces; first pick under 2 meters

parts.name: TCRT5000 infrared line-tracking / obstacle module
parts.buy: TCRT5000 infrared reflective sensor module line tracking obstacle avoidance 5 pack
parts.pins: VCC GND DO AO
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, DO→PB0. It emits an IR beam; a white or nearby object reflects it and DO goes LOW, a black line or nothing nearby doesn't reflect and DO stays HIGH
pitfalls: Sensing range is only 1-2cm; for a line-following robot mount it close to the ground
Sunlight and incandescent bulbs cause false triggers
Adjust sensitivity with the onboard pot, and do it on the actual floor you'll use
parts.note: Must-have for line-following robots; usually buy 2-5

parts.name: HC-SR501 PIR motion sensor
parts.volt: 5V power (4.5-20V); the output is 3.3V and connects directly
parts.buy: HC-SR501 PIR motion sensor module infrared human body detection
parts.pins: VCC OUT GND (facing the pots: left VCC, middle OUT, right GND; check the silkscreen)
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, OUT→PB0. When someone moves it outputs HIGH for a few seconds (adjustable with the onboard pot)
pitfalls: Needs 30-60 seconds to warm up after power-on and triggers randomly during that time
Two pots: one for sensitivity (range), one for hold time. The factory hold time is often several minutes, so turn it down first
It detects moving heat, so a person standing still looks like nobody's there
parts.note: Outputs HIGH when someone moves; makes a motion-activated light

parts.name: MPU6050 6-axis gyroscope + accelerometer GY-521
parts.buy: MPU6050 GY-521 6-axis accelerometer gyroscope module I2C
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA XDA XCL AD0 INT
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, leave the other pins unconnected. Address 0x68 (0x69 with AD0 pulled high)
pitfalls: lib_deps needs adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor and adafruit/Adafruit BusIO
Tilt from the accelerometer alone is only valid at rest; once it moves you need to fuse in the gyroscope (complementary filter). Don't expect to read an angle directly
About 9.8 on the z axis at rest is normal; that's gravity
parts.note: Orientation, vibration, step counting, balancing robots

parts.name: QMC5883L 3-axis compass GY-271
parts.buy: GY-271 QMC5883L 3-axis magnetometer compass module
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA DRDY
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, address 0x0D
pitfalls: Early GY-271 boards used the HMC5883L (address 0x1E); nearly all current ones are QMC5883L (0x0D). The libraries aren't interchangeable, so scan the address first
Keep it away from motors, magnets, speakers, and steel desks or it points everywhere but north
Calibrate on first use by waving it in a figure-8
parts.note: Knows which way it's facing; robot navigation, digital compass

parts.name: BMP280 barometric pressure / temperature module
parts.volt: 3.3V (most modules have an LDO and accept 5V)
parts.buy: BMP280 barometric pressure temperature sensor module GY-BMP280 I2C
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA CSB SDO
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, leave CSB/SDO unconnected. Address 0x76 (0x77 with SDO pulled high)
pitfalls: begin() failing is usually the address: try both 0x76 and 0x77
For altitude you need today's local sea-level pressure, or you'll be off by tens of meters
Some sellers pass off a BMP280 as a BME280 (the BME adds humidity); check the chip marking
parts.note: Computes altitude, also works as an indoor barometer

parts.name: BME280 temperature, humidity & pressure 3-in-1
parts.volt: 3.3V (most modules have an LDO and accept 5V)
parts.buy: BME280 temperature humidity barometric pressure sensor module I2C (Adafruit #2652 is the BME280 breakout)
parts.pins: VIN GND SCL SDA (some also have CSB SDO)
parts.wiring: VIN→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, address 0x76 or 0x77
pitfalls: If you actually got a BMP280, humidity always reads 0; check the chip marking: BME or BMP
Self-heating pushes temperature about 1 degree high; use forced mode and read at intervals
parts.note: A whole mini weather station in one module

parts.name: MQ-2 smoke / flammable gas sensor
parts.volt: 5V (the heater needs 5V); AO can swing to 5V, so divide it down before PA0
parts.buy: MQ-2 gas sensor module smoke flammable gas detection Arduino
parts.pins: VCC GND DO AO
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, AO→1kΩ→PA0, PA0→2kΩ→GND (divides down to under 3.3V); DO→PB8 can connect directly (5V-tolerant)
pitfalls: Needs 2-3 minutes of warm-up; early readings are garbage. For long-term use, burn it in for 24 hours before it's stable
The module gets hot; that's normal (there's a heater inside). It draws 150mA
Readings are relative; they can't be converted to ppm
parts.note: Needs warm-up. 5V device; AO needs a divider

parts.name: MQ-135 air quality sensor
parts.volt: 5V; AO to the ADC through a divider
parts.buy: MQ-135 air quality sensor module harmful gas detection Arduino
parts.pins: VCC GND DO AO
parts.wiring: Same as the MQ-2: VCC→5V, AO through a 1kΩ+2kΩ divider to PA0
pitfalls: The online "MQ135 CO2 ppm" formulas are basically unreliable; it also reacts to alcohol, ammonia, and smoke
Same warm-up requirement, same relative-only readings
parts.note: Good enough for "time to open a window"; for real CO2 numbers buy an SCD40

parts.name: PMS5003 / PMS7003 laser PM2.5 particulate sensor
parts.buy: PMS5003 PM2.5 laser dust particulate sensor Plantower with breakout board (Adafruit carries it)
parts.pins: VCC GND SET RST TX RX (1.25mm ribbon cable to a breakout board)
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, sensor TX→Blue Pill PA3 (RX2), RX→PA2 (TX2), leave SET/RST unconnected
pitfalls: The connector is tiny (1.25mm pitch); be sure to buy one that includes a breakout board
Data is only accurate after the fan has run for 30 seconds
Don't run it continuously somewhere very dusty; it clogs
parts.note: The same sensor used in home air purifiers; the data is trustworthy

parts.name: Sound sensor (microphone module KY-038 / MAX4466)
parts.buy: sound sensor module KY-038 / MAX4466 electret microphone amplifier (Adafruit makes the MAX4466 board)
parts.pins: AO G + DO
parts.wiring: +→3.3V, G→GND, AO→PA0, DO→PB0 (goes LOW past the threshold; set the threshold with the pot)
pitfalls: It only tells you loud vs. quiet; no speech recognition. For voice you need a dedicated module (LD3320 / ESP32 + cloud)
The KY-038's AO is very insensitive and only reacts to claps; to measure ambient volume buy a MAX4466
A single reading is meaningless; measure the peak-to-peak over a short window
parts.note: Clap-on lights, music-reactive LEDs

parts.name: Flame sensor module (infrared, 760-1100nm)
parts.buy: flame sensor module infrared fire detection Arduino 5 pack
parts.pins: VCC GND DO AO
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, DO→PB0 (goes LOW when it sees flame), AO→PA0 (closer flame = lower reading)
pitfalls: Test with a lighter from 30-80cm; don't start an actual fire
Sunlight, incandescent bulbs, and TV remotes all cause false alarms
parts.note: Firefighting robot, fire-alarm demo

parts.name: A3144 Hall effect switch / KY-003 module
parts.volt: 3.3-5V (the A3144 is rated from 4.5V but most work at 3.3V; if not, use an SS49E/3144E module)
parts.buy: A3144 Hall effect sensor switch / KY-003 Hall magnetic sensor module
parts.pins: VCC GND OUT (bare part, facing the printed side: VCC GND OUT)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, OUT→PB0 (INPUT_PULLUP). OUT goes LOW when a magnet comes near
pitfalls: It responds to only one magnetic pole; flip the magnet over and nothing happens
Open-collector output, so the bare part needs a pull-up
More reliable and longer-lived than a reed switch, but it needs power
parts.note: Wheel speed (stick a magnet on the wheel and count pulses), contactless switches

parts.name: ACS712 current sensor module (5A/20A/30A)
parts.volt: 5V power; output is centered at 2.5V, so divide it down before PA0 (or buy the 3.3V version)
parts.buy: ACS712 current sensor module 5A Hall effect Arduino
parts.pins: VCC GND OUT + two large screw terminals in series with the circuit under test
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, OUT→1kΩ→PA0, PA0→2kΩ→GND; cut the load's power wire and connect the two ends to the large terminals (in series)
pitfalls: At zero current the output is 2.5V, not 0; record the no-load reading first and use it as your baseline
The 5A version is only accurate to about ±0.1A; for tens of mA you won't see anything, use an INA219
It goes in series with the circuit; never in parallel
parts.note: Measure motor or battery discharge current. For precise small currents use an INA219

parts.name: INA219 voltage / current / power monitor module
parts.buy: INA219 current voltage power sensor module I2C (Adafruit #904 is the INA219 breakout)
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA VIN+ VIN-
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7; supply positive→VIN+, VIN-→load positive (in series on the positive wire), load GND and module GND tied together (common ground)
pitfalls: VIN+/VIN- go in series on the positive wire; wired in parallel they short out the supply
Address 0x40, changeable via solder jumpers on the back
Maximum 3.2A (with the onboard 0.1Ω sense resistor)
parts.note: Accurate power measurement; for battery projects, work out how long it will run

parts.name: MAX30102 heart-rate / SpO2 sensor module
parts.volt: 3.3V (some modules take 5V on VIN but pull I2C up to 1.8V; watch out for that)
parts.buy: MAX30102 heart rate pulse oximeter sensor module
parts.lib: sparkfun/SparkFun MAX3010x Pulse and Proximity Sensor Library
parts.pins: VIN GND SCL SDA INT
parts.wiring: VIN→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, address 0x57
pitfalls: Rest your finger on it lightly and hold still; press too hard and you squeeze the blood flow away
Some cheap boards tie the I2C pull-ups to 1.8V and the Blue Pill can't read them; move the on-board pull-up resistors to 3.3V or get a different board
Computing SpO2 means running the library's SpO2 example, which is tight on the Blue Pill's RAM
parts.note: Put a finger on it to measure heart rate

parts.name: TCS34725 RGB color sensor
parts.buy: TCS34725 RGB color sensor module; Adafruit carries the original
parts.pins: VIN GND SCL SDA LED INT
parts.wiring: VIN→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7; tie the LED pin to GND to turn off the on-board white LED
pitfalls: Hold it close to the object (within 1cm) and light it with the on-board white LED; ambient light throws it off
Telling red/yellow/blue/green apart is easy; telling similar shades apart needs your own calibration
parts.note: Color sorting, guess-the-color games

parts.name: RC522 RFID reader module + card/key fob
parts.buy: RC522 RFID reader module kit 13.56MHz with card and key fob
parts.pins: SDA(CS) SCK MOSI MISO IRQ GND RST 3.3V
parts.wiring: 3.3V→3.3V, GND→GND, SCK→PA5, MISO→PA6, MOSI→PA7, SDA(CS)→PA4, RST→PB0, leave IRQ unconnected
pitfalls: 3.3V power only; UNO users burn these out all the time
No card detected: run PCD_DumpVersionToSerial first and check the version; 0x00 or 0xFF means a wiring problem
It won't read transit cards or government IDs, only 13.56MHz Mifare cards
parts.note: Tap-to-unlock, check-in systems

parts.name: NEO-6M / NEO-M8N GPS module
parts.volt: 3.3-5V (module has an on-board LDO), serial (UART) is 3.3V
parts.buy: NEO-6M GPS module with ceramic antenna
parts.pins: VCC RX TX GND
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V (or 5V, check the silkscreen), GND→GND, module TX→Blue Pill PA3 (RX2), module RX→PA2 (TX2)
pitfalls: Indoors it almost never sees satellites; take it to a window or outside. The first fix takes 1-5 minutes, and the blue LED starts blinking once it has a fix
Data on the serial port (a stream of $GPGGA lines) but no lat/lon = no fix yet, which is normal
Chinese map services (Amap/Baidu) use shifted coordinates, so a raw fix plotted on them lands a few hundred meters off; Google Maps takes GPS coordinates as-is
parts.note: Track logging, location alerts

parts.name: AS608 optical fingerprint sensor module
parts.buy: AS608 optical fingerprint sensor module
parts.pins: VCC TX RX GND (some also have TOUCH/3.3V touch-sense pins); ribbon cable colors differ by vendor, check the datasheet
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, module TX→PA3 (RX2), module RX→PA2 (TX2)
pitfalls: Enroll fingerprints with the library's enroll example first, then run the match sketch
The 6-wire ribbon cable colors are inconsistent; always check the seller's pinout diagram. Getting VCC wrong fries it instantly
If begin fails, try 9600 baud or check that TX/RX are crossed over
parts.note: Fingerprint lock, fingerprint power-on

parts.name: HX711 load cell amplifier + strain gauge load cell (1kg/5kg)
parts.buy: HX711 load cell amplifier with 5kg load cell kit
parts.pins: VCC GND DT SCK + load cell E+ E- A+ A-
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, DT→PB8, SCK→PB9; load cell red→E+, black→E-, white→A-, green→A+ (go by the seller's diagram for colors)
pitfalls: The load cell must be clamped at one end with the other end free to bend (a lever); laying it flat and pressing on it gives no reading
Calibrate the set_scale factor yourself: put a known 500g weight on it and divide the raw reading by 500
Drifting readings: unstable power or wires too long; use short wires and add a capacitor
parts.note: Digital scale, how much cat food is left, did the package arrive

parts.name: 1-channel relay module (5V, with optocoupler)
parts.volt: 5V supply; get the "active-low" version so 3.3V can drive it reliably. Contacts switch 10A 250V / 10A 30V
parts.buy: 1 channel relay module 5V active low optocoupler isolated
parts.pins: VCC GND IN + contacts COM NO NC
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, IN→PB0; load: supply +→COM, NO→load +, load -→supply -. Write LOW to energize (active-low version). It's just an electrically controlled switch: the GPIO presses the switch, and the contact side can be an entirely separate circuit
pitfalls: Active-high versions often won't latch, or stay stuck on, with 3.3V; buy the active-low kind
Mains voltage (120V/240V AC) is dangerous; while you're learning, only switch 5V/12V loads
The coil draws 70mA when energized; several relays need their own 5V supply
parts.note: Control high-power things like pumps and light bulbs. Mains is dangerous; beginners should only switch 5V/12V loads

parts.name: 4-channel relay module (5V, with optocouplers)
parts.buy: 4 channel relay module 5V active low optocoupler
parts.pins: VCC GND IN1-IN4 JD-VCC + COM NO NC per channel
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, IN1-4→PB12 PB13 PB14 PB15; for full isolation pull the JD-VCC jumper cap and feed JD-VCC from a separate 5V supply
pitfalls: All four energized draw about 300mA; pulling that from the Blue Pill's 5V pin is flaky, use a separate 5V supply
GPIOs float at power-up, so the relays may chatter briefly; write HIGH first thing in setup
parts.note: Multiple lights/pumps/valves

parts.name: Mini submersible water pump + silicone tubing (DC 3-6V)
parts.buy: mini submersible water pump DC 3-6V with silicone tubing
parts.pins: Two wires + - (most have no polarity marking; if it runs backwards, swap the wires)
parts.wiring: Pump +→5V; pump -→MOSFET module V- (or relay NO); MOSFET module SIG→PB0, common ground. Put a 1N5819 across the pump terminals (reverse-biased)
pitfalls: Never connect it directly to a GPIO; 200mA will burn out the pin
It has to be submerged to pump; running it dry moves no water and damages the pump
Powering the pump from the board's USB can make the board reset; add a 1000μF capacitor or use a separate supply
parts.note: Plant-watering projects. Can't drive it from a GPIO directly; needs a relay or MOSFET

parts.name: MOSFET driver module (IRF520 / AOD4184 / D4184)
parts.volt: Triggers from a 3.3V signal (the IRF520 only half-turns-on at 3.3V; for bigger loads pick the D4184 module); load side 0-24V
parts.buy: D4184 MOSFET module / IRF520 MOSFET driver module
parts.pins: SIG GND VCC (optional) + load side V+ V- VIN GND
parts.wiring: SIG→PB0 (PWM), module GND→Blue Pill GND; load supply→VIN/GND, load→V+/V-. Think of it as a water valve: the SIG voltage sets how far it opens
pitfalls: Driven at 3.3V the IRF520 only turns on halfway and gets hot above 1A; the D4184/AOD4184 module is a better match for the Blue Pill
The load GND and the Blue Pill GND must be connected, otherwise SIG has no reference
Put a flyback diode across inductive loads like motors and pumps
parts.note: Quieter than a relay and can vary speed. Drives motors, LED strips, pumps

parts.name: SG90 9g micro servo (plastic gears)
parts.buy: SG90 micro servo 9g 180 degree
parts.pins: Brown GND, red VCC, orange signal
parts.wiring: Brown→GND, red→5V, orange→PB0. One servo can try running from the board's 5V; two or more need a separate 5V supply with common ground
pitfalls: Board resets as soon as the servo moves: not enough current; use a separate supply plus a 1000μF capacitor
write(0) and write(180) don't reach the ends, or it stalls and buzzes: use attach(pin, 500, 2400) to fine-tune the range
Cheap servos don't last long; stalling at the end stops strips the gears, so don't let it push against a hard stop
parts.note: 0-180 degrees. Multiple servos need their own power supply

parts.name: MG996R metal-gear servo (55g, high torque)
parts.volt: 5-7.2V, stall current up to 2.5A, must have its own power supply
parts.buy: MG996R metal gear servo 180 degree high torque
parts.pins: Brown GND, red VCC, orange signal
parts.wiring: Red→+ of a separate 5V 3A supply, brown→supply - and also connected to Blue Pill GND, orange→PB0. Never power it from the Blue Pill's 5V pin
pitfalls: On USB power it resets the moment it moves; you need a separate 5V 3A supply plus a 1000μF capacitor
Many listings are the 360-degree continuous-rotation version, where write controls speed instead of angle; make sure it says "180 degree"
Strong enough to pinch a finger badly; when building a mechanism, test at small angles first and go slowly
parts.note: Needs its own 5V supply; signal goes to a PWM pin, supply ground shares common ground with the controller

parts.name: PCA9685 16-channel servo driver board
parts.volt: Logic 3.3-5V; servo power V+ 5-6V fed in separately
parts.buy: PCA9685 16 channel PWM servo driver I2C (Adafruit #815 for the original)
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA OE + V+ power terminal + 16 sets of 3-pin servo headers
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7; servo power 5V goes to the green screw terminal V+/GND; servos plug onto the 3-pin headers (brown at the bottom)
pitfalls: The V+ supply must be beefy: 16 SG90s moving at once can peak at 10A
The 150/600 in setPWM are pulse-width counts, not degrees; find the range for your servos by trial
parts.note: Robot arms, hexapods; 16 servos on two I2C wires

parts.name: 28BYJ-48 stepper motor + ULN2003 driver board
parts.buy: 28BYJ-48 stepper motor with ULN2003 driver board 5V
parts.pins: Driver board IN1-IN4 + - ; the motor's 5-wire white plug goes straight into the driver board
parts.wiring: IN1→PB12, IN2→PB13, IN3→PB14, IN4→PB15, +→5V, -→GND
pitfalls: Vibrates but doesn't turn: the four wires are in the wrong order; the AccelStepper constructor must be IN1 IN3 IN2 IN4
One revolution is 4096 steps (half-step) or 2048 steps (full-step); the 1:64 gearbox makes it slow but precise
Very little torque, can't push anything heavy; for real force move up to a NEMA17
parts.note: Precise angles, slow. Common in timed-feeder mechanisms

parts.name: NEMA17 stepper motor + A4988/DRV8825 driver
parts.volt: 3.3V logic is fine; motor supply 8-35V (12V is typical)
parts.buy: NEMA17 stepper motor + A4988 stepper driver module
parts.pins: Driver board VMOT GND 2B 2A 1A 1B VDD GND STEP DIR EN MS1-3 SLP RST
parts.wiring: VDD→3.3V, logic GND→GND, STEP→PB0, DIR→PB1, tie SLP to RST; VMOT→12V, motor GND→12V negative (put a 100μF capacitor across VMOT); the motor's four wires go to 1A 1B 2A 2B
pitfalls: Connect the motor before powering up; plugging or unplugging the motor while powered kills the driver
The little trim pot on the driver sets the current limit; left unadjusted it will burn the motor or not turn at all. Start Vref at 0.4V and go up slowly
Without a capacitor across VMOT, the surge when you plug in power can destroy the driver board
parts.note: The motor from 3D printers: strong and precise, for linear slides and robot arms

parts.name: TT DC gear motor + L298N driver board
parts.volt: L298N motor supply 6-12V; logic is 5V but accepts 3.3V inputs
parts.buy: L298N motor driver module + TT gear motor robot car
parts.pins: 12V GND 5V ENA IN1 IN2 IN3 IN4 ENB OUT1-4
parts.wiring: Battery +→12V, battery -→GND and also connected to Blue Pill GND; ENA→PA8 (PWM), IN1→PB12, IN2→PB13; motor to OUT1/OUT2. With the 5V jumper cap in place the board outputs 5V, which can power the Blue Pill
pitfalls: The L298N drops about 2V itself, so a 6V battery leaves only 4V for the motors and the car is sluggish; if the budget allows, switch to a TB6612
Board resets when the motor starts: motor and board share a supply with no filtering; give the motors their own battery
If a motor spins the wrong way, fix it in code, no need to re-solder
parts.note: Robot car projects. Motors need their own battery

parts.name: TB6612FNG dual motor driver module
parts.buy: TB6612FNG dual motor driver module
parts.pins: VM VCC GND STBY PWMA AIN1 AIN2 A01 A02 PWMB BIN1 BIN2 B01 B02
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, STBY→3.3V, VM→motor battery +, PWMA→PA8, AIN1→PB12, AIN2→PB13, motor to A01/A02
pitfalls: If STBY isn't pulled high the motors won't turn; the most common "why is nothing happening"
Much smaller than the L298N, efficient and doesn't get hot, but only 1.2A, so no big motors
parts.note: The modern replacement for the L298N; first choice for robot cars
