parts.name: N20 micro gear motor (encoder optional)
parts.buy: N20 micro gear motor 6V 200RPM / with encoder
parts.pins: Two motor terminals (encoder version adds VCC GND A B)
parts.wiring: Motor terminals to TB6612 A01/A02; encoder VCC→3.3V, A→PB8, B→PB9, count pulses with an interrupt
pitfalls: The speed rating is RPM (revolutions per minute): 200RPM suits a small car, 30RPM suits a slow mechanism
On the encoder version the signal wires run alongside the motor wires, and motor noise makes the count jitter; add a 104 (100nF) capacitor
parts.note: The motor for compact projects; pair it with a TB6612

parts.name: 12V solenoid valve (normally closed, G1/2 or 6mm hose)
parts.buy: 12V solenoid valve normally closed water inlet valve DC12V
parts.pins: Two wires (no polarity)
parts.wiring: 12V adapter +→one valve wire, other valve wire→relay NO, relay COM→12V negative; relay IN→PB0. Put a 1N4007 across the valve terminals (reverse-biased)
pitfalls: "Normally closed" means closed when unpowered, open when powered; for watering systems buy normally closed so it won't leak when the power goes out
It relies on water pressure to open; if the tank is too low there isn't enough pressure and no water flows, so add a pump or some height
12V stays on the relay/MOSFET side only; it must never touch the Blue Pill
parts.note: Watering from tap water or a tank, uses less power than a pump

parts.name: 5V mini fan (4010/5010 DC fan)
parts.buy: 5V cooling fan 4010 DC 2 wire
parts.pins: Red + black - (3-wire versions add a yellow tachometer wire)
parts.wiring: Red→5V, black→MOSFET module V-, MOSFET SIG→PB0; or with an S8050: PB0→1kΩ→B, E→GND, black→C
pitfalls: Can't be connected directly to a GPIO
Below about 30% PWM it may not start spinning; kick it to full speed first, then slow down
parts.note: Temperature-controlled fan project: DHT11 + fan + MOSFET

parts.name: HC-05 / HC-06 Bluetooth serial module (Classic Bluetooth)
parts.volt: VCC 3.6-6V (on-board LDO); the RX pin is 3.3V logic, connect straight to the Blue Pill
parts.buy: HC-05 Bluetooth module master slave serial
parts.pins: STATE RXD TXD GND VCC EN(KEY)
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, module TXD→Blue Pill PA3 (RX2), module RXD→PA2 (TX2). Install a "Bluetooth serial terminal" app on your phone and pair (PIN 1234); whatever you send, the board receives
pitfalls: iPhone won't connect: Apple doesn't expose Classic Bluetooth SPP, so for iPhone use an HM-10 (BLE)
To enter AT mode, hold the small button on the module while powering up; the LED blinks slowly. Fast blinking in normal use means waiting to pair
The HC-06 can only be a slave; the HC-05 can be master or slave
parts.note: The easiest way to send commands from an Android app to the board

parts.name: HM-10 / AT-09 BLE Bluetooth 4.0 module
parts.buy: HM-10 Bluetooth 4.0 BLE module AT-09 CC2541
parts.pins: STATE RXD TXD GND VCC EN
parts.wiring: Wire it to PA2/PA3 just like the HC-05; on the phone connect with LightBlue / nRF Connect or a "BLE serial" app
pitfalls: It looks identical to the HC-05 but the protocol is completely different; Android Classic Bluetooth serial apps can't connect to it, you need a BLE app
Many AT-09 boards run clone firmware, and the AT command set doesn't fully match a genuine HM-10
parts.note: The Bluetooth option that works with iPhone

parts.name: ESP-01S WiFi serial module (AT commands)
parts.volt: 3.3V only! 5V fries it instantly; 300mA peak current, more than the Blue Pill's 3.3V pin can comfortably supply
parts.buy: ESP-01S WiFi module ESP8266 serial
parts.pins: GND GPIO2 GPIO0 RX VCC RST CH_PD(EN) TX (2x4 header, won't plug straight into a breadboard)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V (ideally its own LDO), CH_PD→3.3V, GND→GND, module TX→PA3 (RX2), RX→PA2 (TX2)
pitfalls: You send AT commands one at a time and parse each reply; a single HTTP request takes dozens of lines and is painful
Underpowered, it reboots constantly; garbage on the serial port means not enough current
If you really need networking, switch to an ESP32/ESP8266 as the main controller and let it do the Blue Pill's job too
parts.note: A hassle. If you really need networking, just use an ESP32 as the controller

parts.name: nRF24L01+ 2.4GHz wireless module
parts.volt: 3.3V only! 5V fries it; signal pins are 5V-tolerant
parts.buy: nRF24L01+ 2.4GHz wireless transceiver module / PA+LNA version with antenna
parts.pins: GND VCC CE CSN SCK MOSI MISO IRQ (2x4 header)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V (10μF capacitor across VCC/GND), GND→GND, SCK→PA5, MISO→PA6, MOSI→PA7, CE→PB0, CSN→PA4, leave IRQ unconnected. One module on each of two boards, one transmits and one receives
pitfalls: Nine times out of ten "nothing received" is power: put a 10μF-100μF capacitor across VCC, or buy the adapter base board with a built-in regulator
The 2x4 header won't plug into a breadboard; use female-to-female jumper wires
The PA+LNA version with antenna draws more power; set the PA level to LOW first until the link works
parts.note: Two boards talking to each other over tens of meters; better than Bluetooth for remote control

parts.name: SX1278 LoRa module (433MHz, Ra-01 / Ra-02)
parts.buy: Ra-02 SX1278 LoRa module 433MHz with antenna
parts.pins: GND 3.3V RST DIO0 NSS SCK MOSI MISO + antenna IPEX/SMA
parts.wiring: 3.3V→3.3V, GND→GND, SCK→PA5, MISO→PA6, MOSI→PA7, NSS→PA4, RST→PB0, DIO0→PB1. Always attach the antenna before powering up
pitfalls: Transmitting without an antenna burns out the power amplifier
Very slow (a few hundred bytes per second): fine for sensor numbers, forget about images
Frequency, spreading factor and bandwidth must match on both ends or they won't talk
parts.note: Long-range (a few km) low-speed link: farm fields, a distant water tank

parts.name: 433MHz superregenerative TX/RX pair (+ key-fob remote)
parts.buy: 433MHz RF transmitter receiver module pair superregenerative
parts.pins: Transmitter: DATA VCC GND; receiver: VCC DATA DATA GND
parts.wiring: Receiver VCC→5V, DATA→PB8 (5V-tolerant); transmitter VCC→5V, DATA→PB0. Solder a 17cm piece of single wire next to DATA on each module as an antenna
pitfalls: Without the antenna the range is about 1 meter
One-way, no error checking, lots of noise; only good for simple on/off commands
It can read the codes from your garage door opener or remote-controlled outlets; learn their codes and you can control them
parts.note: The cheapest wireless remote control; reads off-the-shelf 433MHz remotes

parts.name: IR transmitter LED / KY-005 module (940nm)
parts.volt: 1.2-1.5V, needs a current-limiting resistor; the module version takes 3.3V directly
parts.buy: 940nm IR emitter LED 5mm / KY-005 IR transmitter module
parts.pins: Long leg +, short leg - (module: S - +)
parts.wiring: PB0→100Ω→LED long leg, short leg→GND (for more range, drive 2 LEDs in parallel through a transistor)
pitfalls: You can't see it light up, but a phone camera shows a purple glow, which tells you whether it's transmitting
First use an IR receiver to record the target remote's protocol and codes (NEC/Sony/Samsung all differ)
Range is only 2-3 meters; a transistor and several LEDs in parallel get you to about 8 meters
parts.note: Turn the board into a remote for your AC or TV

parts.name: RS485 to TTL module (MAX485 / auto-direction version)
parts.volt: 5V supply (3.3V version uses the MAX3485); DI/RO are 3.3V-compatible
parts.buy: RS485 to TTL converter module MAX485 auto direction
parts.pins: DI DE RE RO VCC GND A B
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, RO→PA3 (RX2), DI→PA2 (TX2), tie DE and RE together→PB0 (drive high to transmit); A/B twisted pair to the other device's A/B, 120Ω termination at the far end
pitfalls: A to A, B to B; swapped, you receive nothing, but nothing breaks
Wait for flush() before pulling DE low after sending, or the last byte gets cut off
Most industrial sensors (temperature/humidity, power meters) speak Modbus RTU, which is another protocol layer to learn
parts.note: Wired links of hundreds of meters; talks to industrial sensors (Modbus)

parts.name: MCP2515 CAN bus module (with TJA1050)
parts.volt: 5V supply (the TJA1050 needs 5V); 3.3V SPI signals are fine, but MISO outputs 5V, so PA6 needs a voltage divider or use the 3.3V version
parts.buy: MCP2515 CAN bus module TJA1050 SPI
parts.pins: INT SCK SI SO CS GND VCC + CAN_H CAN_L
parts.wiring: VCC→5V, GND→GND, SCK→PA5, SI→PA7, SO→PA6 (recommended: 1kΩ+2kΩ voltage divider in series), CS→PA4, INT→PB0; CAN_H/CAN_L to the bus, 120Ω at both ends (on-board jumper J1)
pitfalls: The crystal setting must match the board (8MHz is common, 16MHz exists too); get it wrong and every baud rate is off
To read car OBD data, connect CAN_H/CAN_L to pins 6/14 of the OBD port at 500K baud
A single module can't send and receive to itself without errors; test with at least two nodes or use loopback mode
parts.note: Reading car data, reliable multi-board communication

parts.name: W5500 Ethernet module (wired network)
parts.volt: 3.3V (some modules take 5V in with an LDO), 150mA running current
parts.buy: W5500 Ethernet module SPI lite
parts.pins: GND 3.3V MOSI MISO SCK CS RST INT
parts.wiring: 3.3V→3.3V, GND→GND, SCK→PA5, MISO→PA6, MOSI→PA7, CS→PA4, Ethernet cable to your router
pitfalls: 150mA is a stretch for the Blue Pill's 3.3V pin; add an AMS1117
With no cable plugged in, begin blocks for 60 seconds
Make up your own MAC address, just don't repeat one on the same network
parts.note: For projects that need stability and don't want to fuss with WiFi: go wired

parts.name: PCF8574 I2C I/O expander module (8-bit)
parts.buy: PCF8574 I2C IO expander module 8 bit
parts.pins: VCC GND SDA SCL INT + P0-P7 + A0 A1 A2 address jumpers
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7; P0-P7 to buttons/LEDs. Address 0x20 (A0-A2 all low), up to 8 boards chained
pitfalls: Each pin can sink 25mA when low but sources almost nothing when high, so wire LEDs as "P pin→GND side" (lit when low)
Before reading a button, write(pin, HIGH) to release the pin
parts.note: When you run out of pins: two wires buy you 8 more

parts.name: Level shifter module (TXS0108E 8-channel / 4-channel MOSFET bidirectional)
parts.buy: TXS0108E level shifter module 8 channel 3.3V 5V bidirectional
parts.pins: VA GND A1-A8 OE | VB GND B1-B8
parts.wiring: VA→3.3V, VB→5V, common ground, OE→3.3V; Blue Pill signals on the A side, 5V module signals on the B side, matched one-to-one
parts.snippet:
// No code needed; wire it in and it converts transparently.
// Typical: Blue Pill PB6/PB7 → A1/A2, 5V sensor SCL/SDA → B1/B2
pitfalls: The TXS0108 auto-detects direction but has weak drive; for things like WS2812 use a one-way 74HCT245
The 4-channel MOSFET version (BSS138) only suits slow signals like I2C; high-speed SPI gets distorted
If OE isn't pulled high, every channel is disconnected
parts.note: The translator between 5V modules and a 3.3V board

parts.name: Micro SD card module (SPI)
parts.volt: Modules with an LDO take 5V power with 3.3V signals; the bare 3.3V mini module runs straight from 3.3V
parts.buy: Micro SD card module SPI TF card reader 3.3V
parts.pins: GND VCC MISO MOSI SCK CS
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V (or 5V, depending on the module), GND→GND, SCK→PA5, MISO→PA6, MOSI→PA7, CS→PA4
pitfalls: The card must be FAT32; 32GB and under is most reliable, big cards have compatibility issues
begin fails: wrong CS pin, wires too long, or the card isn't pushed all the way in
Call close() or flush() after every write, or you lose data when the power drops
parts.note: Data logging, storing images/music

parts.name: DS3231 + AT24C32 real-time clock module (large board, with coin cell)
parts.buy: DS3231 AT24C32 real time clock module with battery
parts.pins: 32K SQW SCL SDA VCC GND (one set on each side, can be daisy-chained)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7. The board also has a 4KB AT24C32 EEPROM (address 0x57) for storing settings
pitfalls: If you use a CR2032 (non-rechargeable) coin cell, remove the on-board charging resistor/diode or it may swell; or just buy a rechargeable LIR2032
Wrong time: the adjust line should run only once, then comment it out, otherwise every power-up rolls the clock back to compile time
Address 0x68 conflicts with the MPU6050; tie the MPU6050's AD0 high to move it to 0x69
parts.note: Keeps time through power loss. Timed feeding/watering needs this; comes with a coin cell

parts.name: DS3231SN real-time clock mini board (no EEPROM)
parts.buy: DS3231 RTC module mini for Raspberry Pi
parts.pins: + D C NC - (that is, VCC SDA SCL GND)
parts.wiring: +→3.3V, -→GND, D→PB7 (SDA), C→PB6 (SCL). Same library and same code as the large board
pitfalls: Uses a small CR1220 coin cell; replace it every few years
The silkscreen says + D C NC -, not VCC SDA SCL; don't get confused
Some mini boards carry a DS3231M instead of the SN; slightly less accurate, but you usually won't notice
parts.note: Same chip as the large ds3231 board, just more compact

parts.name: AT24C256 I2C EEPROM module (32KB)
parts.buy: AT24C256 EEPROM memory module I2C
parts.pins: VCC GND SCL SDA WP A0 A1 A2
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, SCL→PB6, SDA→PB7, address 0x50
pitfalls: Each address is good for about 1 million write cycles; don't write every millisecond in loop
Writing one byte takes 5ms; for bulk writes use writeBlock
STM32duino's built-in EEPROM.h emulates EEPROM in Flash; for a handful of settings you don't need to buy this
parts.note: Store settings and calibration values. For small amounts of data the on-chip EEPROM emulation is enough

parts.name: W25Q64 SPI Flash module (8MB)
parts.buy: W25Q64 SPI Flash memory module 8MB
parts.pins: CS DO(MISO) WP GND VCC HOLD CLK DI(MOSI)
parts.wiring: VCC→3.3V, GND→GND, CLK→PA5, DO→PA6, DI→PA7, CS→PA4, WP and HOLD→3.3V
pitfalls: You must erase before writing (in 4KB sectors); erased memory reads all 0xFF
Faster and more reliable than an SD card with no filesystem needed, but you have to plan the address layout yourself
3.3V part; UNO users will fry it
parts.note: Fonts, images, large logs; more dependable than an SD card

parts.name: 18650 Li-ion battery + holder + TP4056 charger board (with 5V boost)
parts.volt: Battery 3.0-4.2V → boosted to 5V, or through an LDO to 3.3V
parts.buy: 18650 battery holder TP4056 charger 5V boost module kit
parts.pins: Charger board: IN+ IN- B+ B- OUT+ OUT-
parts.wiring: Battery→B+/B-, USB charging→IN, OUT+/OUT-→boost board→5V→Blue Pill 5V pin. The 3.7V battery can't go straight to the Blue Pill's 3.3V pin: either boost to 5V into the 5V pin, or drop to 3.3V through a low-dropout LDO
pitfalls: Buy cells with a built-in protection circuit, or a TP4056 with protection (the 6-pin version with the DW01 chip)
Reverse the battery polarity and the TP4056 dies instantly
Never run Li-ion below 3.0V; monitor the voltage and prompt for charging below 3.3V
parts.note: For projects that leave the USB cable behind. The battery needs a protection circuit

parts.name: LiPo battery (3.7V 500-2000mAh, with protection circuit)
parts.buy: 3.7V LiPo battery 1000mAh with protection circuit PH2.0 connector
parts.pins: Red + black - (PH2.0 or JST connector)
parts.wiring: Connect to the TP4056's B+/B-, then run the output through a boost or LDO; some ESP32 dev boards have a battery connector built in
parts.snippet:
// No code. Capacity estimate: Blue Pill 40mA + OLED 20mA ≈ 60mA,
// a 1000mAh battery lasts about 1000/60 ≈ 16 hours
pitfalls: Pouch cells must never be punctured or over-discharged; if one puffs up, stop using it immediately
Connector polarity varies by vendor; match the red/black wire order against the silkscreen on your board
parts.note: Thin and light, the power source for handheld/wearable builds

parts.name: TP4056 Li-ion charger module (Type-C, with protection)
parts.buy: TP4056 charger module Type-C with protection 1A
parts.pins: IN+ IN- B+ B- OUT+ OUT-
parts.wiring: Battery→B+/B-, charge over USB; connect the load to OUT+/OUT- (protected version), not to B+/B-
parts.snippet: // No code. Red LED = charging, blue/green LED = fully charged.
pitfalls: The 6-pin "with protection" version has OUT terminals; the 4-pin version has no protection, so buy the 6-pin one
Resistor R3 on the board sets the charge current; the default 1.2kΩ = 1A. For small batteries (<500mAh) swap in 2kΩ or more, or buy the 500mA version
It isn't great at powering a load while charging (charge-and-use); acceptable for simple projects
parts.note: Charges both 18650 and LiPo cells

parts.name: 5V 2A power adapter (wall adapter) + DC 5.5mm barrel jack adapter
parts.buy: 5V 2A power adapter DC 5.5x2.1mm + DC barrel jack screw terminal adapter
parts.pins: DC jack: + - (center positive, sleeve negative)
parts.wiring: Plug the adapter into the jack, jack +→breadboard 5V rail, -→GND rail; the Blue Pill's 5V pin also goes to the 5V rail. LED strips, servos and pumps all draw from this rail
parts.snippet: // No code. Before you buy, check the output with a multimeter: knockoff adapters labeled 5V have measured 6V.
pitfalls: There are two plug sizes, 5.5x2.1 and 5.5x2.5; buy a jack that takes both
Plugging or unplugging the DC barrel while live sparks; wire everything first, then plug in
Don't power LED strips, motors or pumps from the board's USB
parts.note: Don't power LED strips, motors or pumps from the board's USB

parts.name: 5V 3A power adapter (for servos/motors)
parts.buy: 5V 3A power adapter DC 5.5mm barrel for servo motor
parts.pins: DC 5.5x2.1 center positive, sleeve negative
parts.wiring: Goes through a DC jack to the servo/motor power leads, with GND connected to Blue Pill GND; never put 5V on the Blue Pill's 3.3V pin
parts.snippet: // No code. An MG996R stalls at 2.5A, so even one needs a 3A adapter; for two or more, use a 5V 5A or 6V switching supply.
pitfalls: The Blue Pill and the servo supply must share a common ground, otherwise the servo signal has no reference
Don't treat 5V as a Blue Pill GPIO logic level
parts.note: Powers servos; common ground with the controller

parts.name: 12V 2A power adapter (wall adapter)
parts.buy: 12V 2A power adapter DC 5.5mm barrel
parts.pins: DC 5.5x2.1 center positive, sleeve negative
parts.wiring: Powers 12V LED strips, solenoid valves, NEMA17 steppers and the L298N; add an LM2596 to step down to 5V for the Blue Pill. 12V must never touch any Blue Pill pin
parts.snippet: // No code. One 12V input, an LM2596 splitting off 5V: that's a complete project power supply.
pitfalls: 12V on any Blue Pill pin = dead board
Reversing the input on an L298N/LM2596 burns them too; check the silkscreen first
parts.note: The source for 12V gear (LED strips, valves, big motors)

parts.name: LM2596 adjustable buck converter module (DC-DC step-down)
parts.buy: LM2596 buck converter module adjustable DC-DC with voltmeter display
parts.pins: IN+ IN- OUT+ OUT-
parts.wiring: 12V→IN+/IN-; with no load, turn the trim pot (a dozen or so turns) while measuring OUT with a multimeter until it reads 5.0V, then connect the load. Like a transformer, it "steps down" a high voltage to a low one at 85%+ efficiency
parts.snippet: // No code. Steps: connect input → measure output → trim to 5.00V → power off → connect load → power on.
pitfalls: Always set the voltage before connecting the load; the pot ships at a random position and could put out a full 12V and fry your board
Output must be at least 1.5V below the input: 7V down to 5V works, 5V in for 5V out doesn't
Cheap modules labeled 3A get hot at 1.5A in practice; add a heatsink or derate
parts.note: 12V battery/adapter → 5V for the board

parts.name: MT3608 adjustable boost converter module (DC-DC step-up)
parts.volt: Input 2-24V, output up to 28V, 2A peak (keep continuous under 1A)
parts.buy: MT3608 boost converter module 2A adjustable DC-DC
parts.pins: VIN+ VIN- VOUT+ VOUT-
parts.wiring: Li-ion 3.7V→VIN, turn the trim pot until VOUT reads 5.0V, then feed the Blue Pill's 5V pin. Like a water pump, it "lifts" a low voltage up
parts.snippet: // No code. Fresh out of the bag, the pot needs dozens of counterclockwise turns before the output starts changing; it isn't broken.
pitfalls: Output can't go below the input: 3.7V down to 3.3V isn't a job for this, use an LDO
When boosting, input current = output current × voltage ratio / efficiency; 5V 1A out needs the battery to supply over 1.6A
Voltage sags under heavy load; measure under the actual load first
parts.note: Li-ion 3.7V → 5V for servos/the board

parts.name: AMS1117-3.3 LDO regulator module
parts.volt: Input 4.5-12V, output 3.3V, 800mA max (stay under 500mA in practice or it gets hot)
parts.buy: AMS1117-3.3V voltage regulator module power module
parts.pins: VIN GND VOUT
parts.wiring: 5V→VIN, GND→GND, VOUT→3.3V for power-hungry 3.3V modules like the ESP-01/nRF24. The Blue Pill's on-board LDO only has enough for the board itself
parts.snippet: // No code. With 5V in and 3.3V out, the 1.7V difference becomes heat: at 300mA that's 0.5W, so feeling warm is normal.
pitfalls: The input must be at least 1.2V above 3.3V; straight from a 3.7V Li-ion the output is only about 3.3V and falls short as soon as the battery sags, so use a low-dropout part like the HT7333/ME6211
Don't forget a 10μF capacitor on the output, or it may oscillate
parts.note: Separate power for 3.3V modules, taking the load off the Blue Pill's on-board regulator

parts.name: MB102 breadboard power supply module (3.3V/5V dual rail)
parts.volt: Input DC 6.5-12V or USB 5V; output 3.3V / 5V, 700mA each
parts.buy: MB102 breadboard power supply module 3.3V 5V
parts.pins: Plugs directly onto both power rails of the breadboard; jumper caps select 3.3V/5V/OFF per side
parts.wiring: Plug it into one end of the breadboard power rails, set one side's jumper to 3.3V and the other to 5V, press the switch. Every module's VCC draws from its matching rail, and all GNDs are common
parts.snippet: // No code. Check both rails with a multimeter for 3.3V and 5V before plugging in any modules.
pitfalls: Plugged in backwards (+ and - on the wrong rails) the whole breadboard gets reverse power; check the silkscreen before inserting
On USB power the 5V passes straight through; only the 3.3V is regulated
It takes up the outermost column of holes on the breadboard
parts.note: The easiest way to get both 3.3V and 5V on a breadboard

parts.name: AA battery holder (4 cells 6V / with switch)
parts.buy: 4 x AA battery holder with switch and leads
parts.pins: Red + black -
parts.wiring: 6V can drive an L298N or servos directly; for the Blue Pill go through an LDO or into the 5V pin (the on-board LDO input tolerates 6V), never the 3.3V pin
parts.snippet: // No code. 4 AA cells are about 2000mAh, enough to run a small car's motors for about an hour.
pitfalls: Alkaline cells sag from 6V all the way down to 4V as they discharge, so the motors getting weaker is normal
Don't connect the holder's 6V to the 3.3V pin
parts.note: Simplest for cars and temporary power, but Li-ion is more economical long-term
